```yaml title="my-lab/netdryrun.yml (recorded)"
timeout: 120
checks:
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  afi: ipv4-unicast
  min: 2
  max: 4
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.13.2
# ... the second prefix count, and one route check per learned LAN
- type: route          # a standard guard: no default route via BGP
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
- type: route          # a standard guard: no link subnet via BGP (one per link)
  node: r1
  prefix: 10.0.12.0/30
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
# ... 22 more: the same pattern for r2 and r3
```

!!! tip "A lab you just cloned"
    The recorded file is the lab's steady state, written down. `netdryrun run` deploys the lab from scratch and checks that it reaches that state again. That is useful on its own, before you test any change: after you clone a public lab, bump an image tag, or move the lab to another machine or to CI, a pass says the lab still converges the way it did when you recorded it. A failure names the session or route that didn't come back.

`record` reads BGP. Routes from OSPF, IS-IS, static or connected can be checked too: add `route` checks with `protocol: ospf` (or `isis`, `static`, `connected`) by hand. Checks for the OSPF and IS-IS adjacencies themselves are on the roadmap, not in a release yet.

## 2. Review it

A recorded baseline allows only modest growth: from 0.3.3 each prefix count is today's count as `min` and 20% more (at least 2) as `max` (0.3.2 and earlier recorded `exact`, which failed the day a site added a LAN). Decide what is allowed to change.

- **Keep** every `bgp_session` check.
- **Set the prefix ranges to the growth you expect**, for example `max: 10` where sites are added often. `max` stays a cheap leak guard. `--exact-prefixes` pins exact counts; `--min-prefixes` records minimums only.
- **Keep the standard guards** `record` adds: no default route and no link subnet via BGP on each BGP node. A prefix range has room for one leaked default route; the guard is what catches it.
- **Keep the route checks you care about**, and drop the rest.

Add `--attributes` to `record` if you also want each route's AS path, local preference and communities pinned.

## 3. Add one negative check

From 0.3.3, `record` already adds the two standard guards on every BGP node: no default route via BGP and no link subnet via BGP. Beyond those, it writes down only what exists; it can't know what else must never happen in your network. Add the leak that matters most to you. If your recorded file has no default-route guard (for example, one recorded with `--no-guards`), this is the one to start with:

```yaml title="add under checks:"
- type: route          # nobody sends r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

It fails on a BGP default that r1 received, even one r1 doesn't select, which is why ping and session checks miss it ([the story](../posts/ping-missed-the-leak.md)). More guards to paste, such as link subnets kept out of BGP, a community that must survive, and a neighbor flooding you, are on [Guard recipes](../recipes.md).

Check the file without starting a lab. This is the tutorial's reviewed file, with the default-route check and one more for a link subnet:

```text
$ netdryrun validate my-lab
OK: my-lab/netdryrun.yml (13 checks, lab ~/my-lab/topology.clab.yml, 3 nodes)
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.12.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r2: BGP session to 10.0.23.2 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.13.1 is established
  - [bgp_session] r3: BGP session to 10.0.23.1 is established
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [bgp_prefixes] r1: prefixes from 10.0.13.2 >= 2 and <= 10
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [route] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present
  - [ping] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success
  - [route] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent
  - [route] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent
```

Then run it: `netdryrun run my-lab`. On the unchanged lab, every check should pass. Then make your change and run it again. In the tutorial, a change that announced a new LAN with `redistribute connected` passed every session, the ping and the prefix range, and failed only a negative check:

```text
  [FAIL] r1: route 10.0.23.0/30 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (0.3s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 12 passed, 1 failed (13 checks)
```

Exit code `1`, with the routing table and BGP table output that proved it in the report. [Read the evidence](../tutorial.md#6-read-the-evidence) shows the full report.

## 4. Run it on every pull request

Put the lab folder in your repository (here, `network/`) and add a workflow:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # only for pr-comment
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0
        with:
          path: network/
          pr-comment: true
```

Every pull request that touches `network/` now deploys the lab on the runner, runs the checks, posts the Markdown report as a comment, uploads `report.json`, and fails the job if a check fails. Make the job a required status check to block merges on a failure. Read the [Action security notes](../github-action.md#security-notes) before you run labs from forks.

## What a pass means

A pass says every check in the file held in the lab. It says nothing about behavior no check looks at, and a container lab isn't your production hardware or scale ([what a lab cannot prove](../trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove)). The baseline and the guards are what make a pass worth something; review them like code.

## Next

- [Guard recipes and scenarios](../recipes.md): more negative checks, and failures the network must survive.
- [Tutorial](../tutorial.md): the same path with a failing change, the fix, and the full evidence.
- [AI agents](../ai-agents.md): let an agent run the same test before it proposes a change.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/guides/frr-ci/

# Test an FRR change in CI

You keep FRR configs in git, one `frr.conf` per router. This guide makes every pull request that touches them boot the routers in containerlab with the changed configs, check how they route, and fail the job if something broke. It uses [`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp) and its broken twin [`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken); every output below is from a real run.

## 1. The lab: one folder next to your configs

`examples/frr-bgp` is three FRR routers in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP. The folder holds:

```text
frr-bgp/
  topology.clab.yml      containerlab topology
  configs/r1.conf        one frr.conf per router (r2.conf, r3.conf)
  configs/daemons        which FRR daemons start
  configs/vtysh.conf     one line: service integrated-vtysh-config
  netdryrun.yml          the checks
```

Each router is a plain `linux` node running the FRR image, with the three files bind-mounted where FRR expects them:

```yaml title="topology.clab.yml"
name: ndr-frr-bgp

topology:
  defaults:
    kind: linux
    image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1
  nodes:
    r1:
      binds:
        - configs/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - configs/vtysh.conf:/etc/frr/vtysh.conf
        - configs/r1.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
    # r2 and r3 the same, with their own frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["r1:eth1", "r2:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r2:eth2", "r3:eth1"]
    - endpoints: ["r3:eth2", "r1:eth2"]
```

FRR details that matter here:

- **`daemons` decides what runs.** `bgpd=yes` (and `staticd=yes` for static routes) or BGP never starts. Netdryrun then reports the run as `inconclusive` (exit code `3`), not as a failed change, because no node ever returned BGP state.
- **`vtysh.conf` with `service integrated-vtysh-config`** makes `vtysh` read the single `frr.conf`, which is the file your pull request changes.
- **`eth0` is containerlab's management interface.** Your links start at `eth1`, and `frr.conf` should name those.
- **Pin the image** to the FRR version you run, not `latest`. Behavior and defaults change between releases.

## 2. The checks that matter for FRR

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 90   # seconds each positive check may wait for convergence

checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.13.2
  - type: bgp_prefixes
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
    min: 1
    max: 10          # guards against a route leak flooding r1
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: r1
    source: 192.168.1.1
    target: 192.168.3.1
  - type: bgp_route    # r1 prefers r2's direct path to r2's LAN over the longer path via r3
    node: r1
    prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
    as_path: "65002"
    next_hop: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route        # nothing should send r1 a default route
    node: r1
    prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
    protocol: bgp
    present: false

scenarios:
  - name: r1-r2 link fails
    link_down: {node: r1, interface: eth1}
    checks:
      - type: route        # r2's LAN is still reachable, now via r3
        node: r1
        prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
        protocol: bgp
      - type: bgp_route    # the best path now goes the long way, through r3
        node: r1
        prefix: 192.168.2.0/24
        as_path: "65003 65002"
        next_hop: 10.0.13.2
      - type: ping
        node: r1
        source: 192.168.1.1
        target: 192.168.2.1
      - type: bgp_session  # and the session over the failed link is really down
        node: r1
        neighbor: 10.0.12.2
        state: down        # any state except established
```

On FRR, each check type reads a different part of the router, and the differences are where changes go wrong:

| Check | Reads | Why it matters on FRR |
|---|---|---|
| `bgp_session` | `show bgp neighbors json` | An `Established` session can still carry nothing. Never use it alone |
| `bgp_prefixes` | `acceptedPrefixCounter` in `show bgp neighbors json` | Counts prefixes after your inbound policy. A filter that drops everything shows here first. `max` is a cheap leak guard |
| `route` | `show ip route <prefix> json` (zebra) | Selected and installed. zebra keeps the losing entries too, so `present: false` also fails on a route that was received but lost |
| `bgp_route` | `show bgp ipv4 unicast <prefix> json` (bgpd) | The best path's AS path, next hop, local preference, MED, communities. Catches a change that still delivers the route, but the long way |
| `ping` | `ping -I <source>` in the container | The data plane, from the source address you give |

BGP's best path and zebra's selected route are not the same thing. A default route leaked by a peer is `*>` (best) in `show bgp ipv4 unicast`, because the static it loses to isn't a BGP path, and it is not selected in `show ip route`. Read the table that answers your question: `bgp_route` for "which path does BGP prefer", `route` for "what does the router forward with". The [hidden leak lab](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak) shows both side by side.

## 3. Run it locally

```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 7 checks from examples/frr-bgp/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-frr-bgp (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.5s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- 2 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2 -- best path: as-path '65002', next hop 10.0.12.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
  [PASS] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.3s)
Scenario: r1-r2 link fails
  the fault took effect after 0s (2 BGP session(s) over the downed links are down)
  settling 10s before the scenario's checks
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: route 192.168.2.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (held 12s, 3 samples) (19.4s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: ping 192.168.2.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (held 12s, 3 samples) (19.4s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: BGP best path for 192.168.2.0/24 has as-path '65003 65002', next hop 10.0.13.2 -- best path: as-path '65003 65002', next hop 10.0.13.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
  [PASS] [r1-r2 link fails] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is down -- state is active (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.0s)
Restored 1 link(s) and 0 route injection(s); settling 10s
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed (11 checks)
```

The `bgp_route` checks run with the post-convergence checks and must hold for 10 seconds, because the best path can change when a slower session comes up. In the scenario, Netdryrun first waits until both ends of the BGP session over the downed link see it down (here at once, because the interface itself went down), settles 10 seconds, and then the positive checks must keep passing for the hold window, not just once. See [scenario timing](../reference/config.md#scenario-timing).

Now the broken change. `frr-bgp-broken` is the same triangle, but r2's config adds one line, `neighbor 10.0.12.1 default-originate`, toward r1:

```bash
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 6 checks from examples/frr-bgp-broken/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-frr-broken (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.5s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.2s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

Sessions are up, the prefix count is within its limit, and the ping works: the LANs have more specific routes, so a default route changes nothing for them. r1 doesn't even select the leaked default, because in this lab it loses to containerlab's management default route (see [Gotchas](#gotchas)). The `present: false` check fails anyway, because zebra still holds the losing BGP entry, and the run exits with `1`.

## 4. Run it on every pull request

```yaml title=".github/workflows/network-dryrun.yml"
name: Network dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/**"
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # for pr-comment
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0
        with:
          path: network/        # the folder with netdryrun.yml
          pr-comment: true
```

The job installs containerlab and Netdryrun, pulls the FRR image, runs the checks, uploads the JSON and JUnit reports, and fails if a check fails. With `pr-comment: true` it also posts the verdict and the evidence for each failed check on the pull request. See [GitHub Action](../github-action.md) for every input, and the security notes before running labs from forks.

**Other CI systems:** any Linux runner that can start privileged Docker containers works. The steps are the same three commands. `env "PATH=$PATH"` keeps the `netdryrun` that `pip` installed on the path under `sudo`:

```bash
bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get.containerlab.dev)" -- -v 0.81.1
pip install netdryrun
sudo env "PATH=$PATH" netdryrun run network/ --junit netdryrun-junit.xml --json netdryrun-report.json
```

Exit codes: `0` passed, `1` a check failed, `2` a setup problem (bad YAML, the lab didn't start), `3` inconclusive (the lab never reached a testable state; rerun it).

## Times

Wall-clock for `netdryrun run`, including deploying and destroying the lab, with images already pulled. Measured on 2026-10-28 on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB), containerlab 0.81.1, Netdryrun 0.3.1 installed from PyPI, running the two example folders of a fresh clone:

| Run | Result | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/frr-bgp` (7 checks and a link-failure scenario) | `PASSED: 11 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 105 s |
| `examples/frr-bgp-broken` | `FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed` | `1` | 41 s |

The failing run is shorter because it has no failure scenario. `frr-bgp` takes longer than on 0.3.0 (88 s) because 0.3.1 settles 10 s after the fault and holds the scenario's checks for a full window, instead of judging them as soon as they pass. The [examples page](../examples.md) shows 99 s and 39 s for the same two labs from the 0.3.1 release check on the same machine the day before; runs differ by several seconds. On GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, the whole job (installing containerlab and Netdryrun, pulling FRR, running) took 100 to 107 s for `frr-bgp` and 54 to 66 s for `frr-bgp-broken`, over three CI runs on `main` on 2026-10-27, before the 0.3.0 release added a `bgp_route` check to `frr-bgp`; see [the FAQ](../faq.md#how-long-does-a-run-take-and-what-does-ci-cost). On a private repository, jobs are billed by the minute, rounded up: the `frr-bgp` job uses 2.

## Gotchas

- **eBGP without a policy may exchange nothing.** Under FRR's default `traditional` profile, `bgp ebgp-requires-policy` is on (RFC 8212): an eBGP neighbor with no route-map in or out reaches `Established` and accepts and sends nothing. Under `frr defaults datacenter`, which the examples use, it's off. On FRR 10.4.1 with no route-maps, the `traditional` side shows:

    ```text
    Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt Desc
    10.9.0.2        4      65002        12        11        1    0    0 00:00:24     (Policy) (Policy) FRRouting/10.4.1_git
    ```

    A `bgp_session` check passes either way; `bgp_prefixes` and `route` checks catch it. Keep the same `frr defaults` line in the lab as in production.
- **containerlab gives `linux` nodes a default route** via the management network. FRR sees it as a kernel route with distance 0, which beats a static or BGP default. If your change or your checks involve the default route, delete it with `exec: ["ip route del default"]` on the node, as the [hidden leak lab](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak) does.
- **Lab names are global on a machine.** Two jobs on one self-hosted runner, or two copies of a folder, must use different `name:` values in `topology.clab.yml`.
- **`frr.conf` is read at boot.** Netdryrun deploys a fresh lab on every run, so the pull request's file is always the one tested. If you poke at a lab kept with `--keep`, changes you make in `vtysh` are not in the file.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/guides/sonic-ci/

# Test a SONiC change in CI

SONiC is different from most network OSes in a lab: the virtual switch image boots with no configuration, and its services come up one by one after the container starts. This guide shows how to get the image, configure the switch once it's ready, and check its routing on every pull request. It uses [`examples/sonic-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/sonic-frr): a SONiC VS switch peering eBGP with an FRR router. Every output below is from a real run.

## 1. Get the image

`docker-sonic-vs` is the virtual switch the SONiC project builds for its own tests. It is not on a container registry: the SONiC build server publishes it as a compressed file. Download it and load it into Docker:

```bash
curl -L -o docker-sonic-vs.gz \
  "https://sonic-build.azurewebsites.net/api/sonic/artifacts?branchName=master&platform=vs&target=target/docker-sonic-vs.gz"
docker load -i docker-sonic-vs.gz      # creates docker-sonic-vs:latest
```

The file is about 230 MB (232,075,139 bytes for the build used on this page, downloaded on 2026-10-27). Loaded, the image is 1.92 GB.

The image carries its build id in a label (`docker image inspect docker-sonic-vs:latest --format '{{index .Config.Labels "Tag"}}'`, for example `master.1258173-c10162df4`). `examples/sonic-frr` pins the build the SONiC driver is verified on, so after loading, tag your image with its build id (`docker tag docker-sonic-vs:latest docker-sonic-vs:<build id>`) and put that tag on the example's image line. `scripts/get_sonic_vs.sh` in the repository does the download and the tag in one step.

`branchName=master` is the latest build, so it changes over time. For repeatable CI, keep the file you tested with (as a release asset or in a cache) instead of downloading `master` on every run.

## 2. The lab

```yaml title="topology.clab.yml"
name: ndr-sonic-frr

topology:
  nodes:
    sonic1:
      kind: sonic-vs
      image: docker-sonic-vs:latest
    frr1:
      kind: linux
      image: quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.4.1
      binds:
        - configs/daemons:/etc/frr/daemons
        - configs/vtysh.conf:/etc/frr/vtysh.conf
        - configs/frr1.conf:/etc/frr/frr.conf
  links:
    - endpoints: ["sonic1:eth1", "frr1:eth1"]
```

In `kind: sonic-vs`, the container's `eth1` is the SONiC port `Ethernet0`. The topology names `eth1`; SONiC commands and checks use `Ethernet0`.

## 3. Configure SONiC after boot: `setup`

There's no startup config. Instead, `netdryrun.yml` lists `setup` commands that Netdryrun runs inside the node after deploying the lab and before any check:

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 180

nodes:
  sonic1:
    setup:
      - supervisorctl status orchagent | grep -q RUNNING && supervisorctl status bgpd | grep -q RUNNING
      - config interface ip add Ethernet0 10.0.40.1/30 && config interface startup Ethernet0
      - config loopback add Loopback0; config interface ip add Loopback0 192.168.40.1/32
      - >-
        vtysh -c "conf t" -c "router bgp 65040" -c "bgp router-id 40.40.40.40" -c "no bgp ebgp-requires-policy"
        -c "neighbor 10.0.40.2 remote-as 65020" -c "address-family ipv4 unicast" -c "network 192.168.40.1/32"
```

Line by line:

1. **Wait for the services.** The container is "running" long before SONiC is. `orchagent` (which programs the switch) and `bgpd` (FRR inside SONiC) have to be `RUNNING` before `config` commands and `vtysh` work. This line fails until they are.
2. **Address and enable the port** with SONiC's `config` CLI, which writes to CONFIG_DB like on a real switch.
3. **A loopback** for the announced prefix.
4. **BGP**, configured in the FRR that runs inside SONiC, through `vtysh`.

Each line is retried every 5 seconds until it succeeds, within a shared budget of 300 seconds. A line runs again from the start if any part of it fails, so put the part that can fail first (as line 1 does), and keep lines that change state safe to run twice.

## 4. The checks that matter for SONiC

```yaml
checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: sonic1
    neighbor: 10.0.40.2
  - type: route
    node: sonic1
    prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
    protocol: bgp
  - type: route
    node: frr1
    prefix: 192.168.40.1/32
    protocol: bgp
  - type: ping
    node: sonic1
    source: 192.168.40.1
    target: 192.168.20.1
  - type: bgp_prefixes
    node: frr1
    neighbor: 10.0.40.1
    min: 1
    max: 5
  - type: bgp_route
    node: sonic1
    prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
    as_path: "65020"
    local_pref: 100
    next_hop: 10.0.40.2

scenarios:
  - name: SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down
    link_down: {node: sonic1, interface: Ethernet0}
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_session, node: frr1, neighbor: 10.0.40.1, state: down}
      - {type: route, node: frr1, prefix: 192.168.40.1/32, protocol: bgp, present: false}
```

What to know about these on SONiC:

- **Routing state comes from the FRR inside SONiC.** The `sonic` driver reads sessions, routes and BGP paths through `vtysh`, exactly as on FRR. A route check says what SONiC's routing stack selected. It does not read what `orchagent` programmed (APPL_DB, ASIC_DB).
- **`ping` covers the data path.** It runs from the switch with the loopback as source, so it only passes if the port, its address and the route all work. Keep at least one ping per change.
- **Check from the other side too.** `route` and `bgp_prefixes` on `frr1` prove what SONiC actually announces, which is what a policy change on the switch affects.
- **A port-down scenario uses the SONiC name.** `link_down` on `Ethernet0` takes the port down inside the switch. The scenario then checks that the peer sees the session drop and the route withdrawn, and Netdryrun brings the port back afterwards.
- **Give it time.** `timeout: 180` covers the slow boot; the `setup` budget is separate.

## 5. Run it locally

```bash
pip install netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/sonic-frr
```

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 6 checks from examples/sonic-frr/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-sonic-frr (2 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
Running setup on sonic1...
setup done on sonic1 (4 commands)
  [PASS] sonic1: BGP session to 10.0.40.2 is established -- state is established (13.7s)
  [PASS] sonic1: route 192.168.20.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.7s)
  [PASS] frr1: route 192.168.40.1/32 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.7s)
  [PASS] sonic1: ping 192.168.20.1 from 192.168.40.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.7s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] frr1: prefixes from 10.0.40.1 >= 1 and <= 5 -- 1 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
  [PASS] sonic1: BGP best path for 192.168.20.0/24 has as-path '65020', local-pref 100, next hop 10.0.40.2 -- best path: as-path '65020', next hop 10.0.40.2, local-pref 100, MED 0, communities none (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.2s)
Scenario: SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down
  the fault took effect after 0s (1 BGP session(s) over the downed links are down)
  settling 10s before the scenario's checks
  [PASS] [SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down] frr1: BGP session to 10.0.40.1 is down -- state is connect (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.1s)
  [PASS] [SONiC port Ethernet0 goes down] frr1: route 192.168.40.1/32 via bgp is absent -- absent (held 10s, 4 samples) (10.1s)
Restored 1 link(s) and 0 route injection(s); settling 10s
Destroying lab...
PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed (8 checks)
```

## 6. Run it on every pull request

The workflow is the usual one with one extra step: load the image before Netdryrun deploys the lab. containerlab only pulls images that are missing, so the loaded `docker-sonic-vs:latest` is used as is.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/sonic-dryrun.yml"
name: SONiC dry run
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "network/sonic/**"
jobs:
  dryrun:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Load docker-sonic-vs
        run: |
          curl -fsSL -o docker-sonic-vs.gz \
            "https://sonic-build.azurewebsites.net/api/sonic/artifacts?branchName=master&platform=vs&target=target/docker-sonic-vs.gz"
          docker load -i docker-sonic-vs.gz
      - uses: netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0
        with:
          path: network/sonic/
```

On other CI systems: load the image the same way, then install containerlab and Netdryrun and run `sudo env "PATH=$PATH" netdryrun run <folder>`, as in the [FRR guide](frr-ci.md#4-run-it-on-every-pull-request).

This workflow is a recipe, not something Netdryrun's own CI runs yet: SONiC isn't in the project's CI, and the workflow hasn't been run on a hosted runner. The runs on this page are local.

## Times

Wall-clock for `netdryrun run`, including deploying the lab, the `setup` lines, the checks, the port-down scenario and destroying the lab, with both images already loaded. Measured on 2026-10-28 on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB), containerlab 0.81.1, Netdryrun 0.3.1 installed from PyPI, running the example folder of a fresh clone:

| Run | Result | Exit | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/sonic-frr` (6 checks and a port-down scenario) | `PASSED: 8 passed, 0 failed` | `0` | 99 s |

The positive checks passed 13.7 s after `setup` finished. The [examples page](../examples.md) shows 92 s from the 0.3.1 release check on the same machine the day before; runs differ by a few seconds. In CI, add the time to download the 230 MB image, which depends on the runner's network; caching the file avoids it.

## Gotchas

- **"Running" isn't ready.** The container is up long before SONiC's services are, and `config` and `vtysh` don't work until they are. Make the first `setup` line a readiness check, so every later line starts on a ready switch.
- **`no bgp ebgp-requires-policy`.** With it on (RFC 8212, FRR's default profile), an eBGP neighbor with no route-map comes up and exchanges nothing; see the [FRR guide's gotchas](frr-ci.md#gotchas). The example turns it off to stay short. With real policies, attach route-maps instead.
- **The image is big and not on a registry.** About 230 MB to download and 1.92 GB once loaded. Cache it in CI.
- **Port names differ between the topology and the switch:** `eth1` in `topology.clab.yml`, `Ethernet0` in SONiC commands, checks and scenarios.
- **Memory:** about 300 MiB for the SONiC VS node once up ([FAQ](../faq.md#how-much-memory-and-cpu-does-it-need)).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/guides/agent-pr/

# AI agents without Docker: the pull-request path

The [MCP server](../ai-agents.md) needs Docker and containerlab on the machine the agent runs on. Many coding agents run in a sandbox without them. They can still get a verdict: they push their change to a branch and open a pull request, the [GitHub Action](../github-action.md) runs the lab on a GitHub runner, and the agent reads the result. This page is that flow, from 0.3.3.

## 1. The workflow in the network repository

```yaml
# .github/workflows/netdryrun.yml
name: Netdryrun
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write      # for the comment
jobs:
  verdict:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false   # the lab runs privileged containers: leave no token in .git/config
      - uses: netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0
        with:
          path: network/        # the folder with netdryrun.yml
          pr-comment: true
```

The job fails on anything but a pass, so branch protection can require it. A pull request from a fork can't be commented on (GitHub gives fork runs a read-only token); the verdict is still in the job result and the artifact.

## 2. What the agent reads

**The comment.** The Action posts one comment per lab (per `path:`) and updates it on every push. Its first lines have a fixed format:

```text


**Netdryrun: DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE** · status `failed` · 5 passed, 1 failed · commit `4f2a9c1e0b7d`
```

Read the JSON on the second line and decide on `status`, with three rules:

- **Only comments by `github-actions[bot]`** (or the account you set as `comment-author`). Anyone can post a comment that looks like this one.
- **Only a header whose `commit` is the pull request's head commit.** A header with an older commit is from an earlier push: wait for the new run. A run that wrote no report still rewrites the header, as `error`.
- **Every Netdryrun comment on the pull request must say `passed`**, one per lab.

The rest of the comment is the human summary: failed checks first, with their evidence.

**The artifact.** For the full detail, the job uploads `netdryrun-verdict.json` with the reports (artifact `netdryrun-report`). It is the same object the MCP tools return: `status`, the frozen `verdict`, `failures` with a reason, an evidence excerpt and a read-only `next_diagnostic` command for each failed check, and `tested`, a sha256 of `netdryrun.yml`, the topology and every config file the run used. Schema: [mcp-result-v1.json](https://netdryrun.com/schemas/mcp-result-v1.json).

## 3. What the agent does with it

- **`passed`**: propose the change, and say the pass covers only what the checks look at (`CHECKS PASSED (only what the checks cover)`).
- **`failed`**: read `failures`, fix the config, push again. The comment updates in place. Never edit `netdryrun.yml` to make a change pass.
- **`inconclusive`** or **`error`**: a setup problem that says nothing about the change. Push no fix for it; report it to the human.

The verdict applies to the commit the job ran on. After any push, wait for the new run.

## Paste this into the repository's AGENTS.md

```markdown
Network changes in this repository are dry-run by Netdryrun on every pull request. After you push, wait for
the "Netdryrun" check, then read the second line of each Netdryrun comment by github-actions[bot] (a JSON
object) whose `commit` is the head commit, and act on its `status`: propose the change only on `passed`; on `failed`, fix the config and push again; on `inconclusive`
or `error`, stop and tell the human. Never edit `netdryrun.yml` to make a change pass.
```


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/reference/config/

# netdryrun.yml reference

`netdryrun.yml` describes one lab and the behavior you expect from it. Commands accept either the file or the folder that contains it (`netdryrun run network/` reads `network/netdryrun.yml`).

```yaml title="netdryrun.yml"
lab: topology.clab.yml
timeout: 90
nodes:
  r1:
    driver: frr
checks:
  - type: bgp_session
    node: r1
    neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  - type: route
    node: r1
    prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
    protocol: bgp
    present: false
```

Validation is strict, and every problem is an error (exit code `2`) before anything is deployed. Run `netdryrun validate` to check a file without starting a lab. From 0.3.1:

- **Unknown keys are errors at every level**: the top level, `nodes.<node>`, checks, scenarios, `link_down`, `node_isolated` and `inject_routes`. A misspelled key gets a suggestion: `unknown keys ['presnt'] for type route; did you mean 'present'?`. Before 0.3.1, a misspelled key at the top level, under `nodes` or inside a fault was ignored, so a misspelled block of checks never ran (keys inside a check or a scenario were already refused).
- **Duplicate keys are errors**, at any depth: `duplicate key 'present' (first defined on line 12)`. Plain YAML keeps the last one silently. The topology file is read the same way. YAML merge keys (`<<: *anchor`) are allowed.
- **Malformed YAML** is reported on one line, with its position: `netdryrun.yml: not valid YAML at line 7, column 3: ...`.
- **Booleans must be real booleans**: `present` and `active` take unquoted `true` or `false`. A quoted `"false"`, `0`, `null` or an empty value is refused instead of being read as something else.
- **Values come from fixed lists** where the drivers only understand certain values: `type`, `state`, `afi`, `protocol`, `expect` and `nodes.<node>.driver`. A near miss gets a suggestion (`afi: ipv4` → `did you mean 'ipv4-unicast'?`).
- **Numbers are range-checked**: see the tables below. Required keys missing, IP addresses that don't parse, and keys that make no sense together (`min_replies` with `expect: failure`, `hold` on a check where it has no effect) are errors too.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lab` | yes | | Path to the containerlab topology file, relative to `netdryrun.yml`. The topology must have a `name`. |
| `timeout` | no | `120` | Seconds a check may wait (see [convergence semantics](#convergence-semantics)). A positive number, at most `86400`. Each check can override it. |
| `checks` | yes | | List of checks. At least one is required. |
| `nodes` | no | | A mapping of node name to settings. Each node accepts only `driver` and `setup`. |
| `nodes.<node>.driver` | no | detected | Force the driver for a node: `frr`, `srlinux`, `eos`, `sonic` or `junos` (Juniper cJunosEvolved, beta). See [drivers](#drivers). |
| `nodes.<node>.setup` | no | | Shell commands run inside the node after deploy, before any check. Each is retried every 5 s until it succeeds (the NOS may still be booting), within a shared 300 s budget. For NOSes that are configured after boot, such as SONiC. |
| `scenarios` | no | | A non-empty list of [failure scenarios](#failure-scenarios). |

No other top-level key is accepted.

## Keys every check accepts

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | required | `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes`, `route`, `bgp_route` or `ping` |
| `node` | required | Node name from the topology (for example `r1`) |
| `name` | generated | Label used in reports. The default describes the check, for example `r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established`. |
| `timeout` | top-level `timeout` | Seconds this check may wait to pass. A positive number, at most `86400`. |
| `hold` | `--hold` (10) | Seconds a [post-convergence check](#convergence-semantics) must hold. A positive number, at most `86400`. Only allowed on post-convergence checks: on any other check it would have no effect, so it is an error. |
| `vrf` | `default` | VRF (FRR, SONiC, Arista EOS) or network-instance (SR Linux) to look in. Letters, digits and `. _ : -`, at most 64 characters: the name goes into the device's CLI command, so anything else is refused (0.3.1 and later; 0.3.0 did not check it). `vrf: all` is refused: name one VRF per check. A VRF that doesn't exist on the node is an error on every driver, never "no routes" (see [drivers](#drivers)). |

Each check type accepts only these keys and the ones in its own table.

IP addresses and prefixes are normalized, so `2001:db8:0::1` in YAML matches `2001:db8::1` on the device. Prefixes with host bits set are reduced to the network (`10.0.0.1/24` becomes `10.0.0.0/24`).

## Check types

### bgp_session

A BGP session reaches a state.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address as configured on `node`. A link-local address that several sessions share (`fe80::1` on two interfaces) is ambiguous: the check is not evaluated, so use a global address |
| `state` | no | `established` | One of `idle`, `connect`, `active`, `opensent`, `openconfirm`, `established`, or `down` (any state except established). Case-insensitive |

The check fails if the neighbor is not configured. A `state` other than `established` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_session
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
```

### bgp_prefixes

The number of prefixes accepted from a neighbor is within a range. Accepted means received minus rejected by import policy.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `neighbor` | yes | | Neighbor IP address (a link-local address several sessions share is ambiguous, as for `bgp_session`) |
| `min` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Lower bound, inclusive |
| `max` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Upper bound, inclusive |
| `exact` | one of `min`, `max`, `exact` | | Exact count |
| `afi` | no | `ipv4-unicast` | Address family: exactly one of `ipv4-unicast`, `ipv6-unicast` or `evpn` (case-insensitive). `evpn` is supported on FRR and SONiC only, not on SR Linux, Arista EOS or Juniper (beta) |

Rules:

- At least one of `min`, `max` or `exact` is required.
- `exact` cannot be combined with `min` or `max`.
- `min` must not be greater than `max`.
- All three are non-negative integers.
- `min: 0` on its own is refused: it always passes. Use `min: 1` or more, or add `max`.
- Any other `afi` is refused (from 0.3.1). An address family the drivers don't report would read as 0 prefixes, which passes `max` and `exact: 0`.
- `afi: evpn` on an SR Linux or Arista EOS node is refused before the lab deploys (exit code `2`): those drivers read only the IPv4 and IPv6 unicast counts (SR Linux has no received-routes counter for EVPN), so an EVPN count would always read 0. SR Linux refuses it from 0.3.1; before, the count read 0 and passed `max`.
- The session must be `established`. Counters reset to 0 when a session drops, so a count from a down session would satisfy `max` by accident; Netdryrun fails the check instead.
- If the session is established but the address family reports nothing, the count is 0.
- A check with `max` or `exact` is a post-convergence check. A check with only `min` is a positive check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_prefixes
  node: r1
  neighbor: 10.0.12.2
  min: 1
  max: 10          # guards against a route leak flooding r1
```

### route

A route is present in (or absent from) the routing table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means the route must be absent. Unquoted `true` or `false` only |
| `protocol` | no | any | Only count routes from this protocol: one of the names in [protocol names](#protocol-names). Case-insensitive |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |
| `active` | no | `true` | With `present: true`: `false` also accepts a route that is in the table but not selected (for example a BGP default losing to a local one). Unquoted `true` or `false` only; not allowed with `present: false` |

- **Present** means an *active* route matches: selected and installed on FRR, `active` on SR Linux.
- **Absent** means no matching route at all, active or not. A BGP path that was received from a neighbor still counts as present, valid or not, selected or not (for example a leaked default losing to a local one), so `present: false` fails. This is how the [failing example](../index.md#a-failing-run) is caught. Every driver reads the BGP table for this as well as the routing table; there, only paths received from a neighbor count, not the router's own (network statements, redistribution, SR Linux's static and interface routes).
- `protocol` must be a name the drivers report. `ebgp` and `ibgp` are refused: drivers report both as `bgp`. A name outside the list would match nothing and silently pass `present: false`.
- `present: false` makes it a post-convergence check.

```yaml
- type: route
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.3.0/24
  protocol: bgp
```

### bgp_route

Attributes of the BGP **best path** for a prefix: communities, AS path, local preference, MED, next hop. Many real policy bugs live here: a route that is still present but lost its community, got the wrong local preference, or now goes the long way. `route` reads the routing table; `bgp_route` reads the BGP table.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prefix` | yes | | IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, matched exactly |
| `communities` | no | | The best path must carry **all** of these. Standard (`'65000:100'`), large (`'65000:1:2'`) or well-known names (`no-export`, `no-advertise`, `no-peer`, `blackhole`, `graceful-shutdown`, `accept-own`, `llgr-stale`, `no-llgr`, `no-export-subconfed`) |
| `without_communities` | no | | The best path must carry **none** of these. Same forms as `communities` |
| `as_path` | no | | Exact AS path, ASNs separated by spaces: `"65002 65003"`. `""` is the empty path of a locally originated route. AS sets are written `{65004,65005}` |
| `as_path_regex` | no | | Python regular expression searched in the AS path string, for example `"^65002 "` (learned from 65002) or `"(^| )65666( |$)"` (passes through 65666). It runs with no time limit, so avoid nested repeats such as `(\d+ ?)+$` that can backtrack for minutes |
| `local_pref` | no | | Exact local preference |
| `med` | no | | Exact MED. A path with no MED attribute fails the check, even `med: 0`: with `bgp bestpath med missing-as-worst` a missing MED is the worst, not 0. On Arista EOS, `med: 0` is refused before the lab boots (exit `2`): cEOS prints MED 0 for a path received with no MED, so the two can't be told apart; a non-zero MED is checked as usual |
| `next_hop` | no | | Exact next hop address. A link-local address is refused: devices report it without its interface, and two sessions can share one, so the check couldn't say which path it tests |
| `present` | no | `true` | `false` means no path at all for the prefix in the BGP table, best or not, valid or not. Unquoted `true` or `false` only |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | VRF or network-instance |

Rules:

- Without attribute keys, the check passes when a best path exists.
- **Quote communities.** YAML reads some unquoted values as numbers (`65000:10` is a base-60 number to YAML 1.1), so an unquoted community that YAML turns into a number is a config error.
- A community can't be in both `communities` and `without_communities`.
- `present: false` can't be combined with attribute keys. To forbid a community on the best path, use `without_communities`.
- The check fails if there is no path, or no best path (for example when the next hop is unreachable). The failure detail shows what the best path actually carries.
- **Local preference** is the effective value: a path without a LOCAL_PREF attribute (eBGP-learned or local) gets the device's default (FRR and SONiC: `bgp default local-preference`; SR Linux: the neighbor's `local-preference`; Arista EOS reports it directly). The exception is a locally originated path on Arista EOS, which reports no local preference; asserting `local_pref` on it fails with "not set".
- **Next hop** is the address the device reports. For an IPv6 path FRR may list only the link-local next hop.
- `present: false`, and any attribute key (`communities`, `without_communities`, `as_path`, `as_path_regex`, `local_pref`, `med`, `next_hop`), make it a post-convergence check. The best path can change when a slower session comes up, so an attribute check could pass on a temporary best path before the real one arrives; it is judged only after every BGP session on the node is up and the settle delay, and must hold (0.3.1 and later; 0.3.0 judged attribute checks other than `without_communities` on 2 early samples). A `bgp_route` with no attribute keys (the best path exists) is a positive check.

```yaml
- type: bgp_route         # customer routes are tagged and preferred
  node: r1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  communities: ["65000:100", no-export]
  local_pref: 200
  as_path: "65020"

- type: bgp_route         # the internal tag must never reach the peer
  node: peer1
  prefix: 192.168.20.0/24
  without_communities: ["65000:666"]
```

### ping

Reachability from a node.

| Key | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | yes | | Destination IP address |
| `source` | no | | Source IP address (passed as `ping -I`) |
| `expect` | no | `success` | `success` or `failure` |
| `count` | no | `3` | Packets to send. An integer from 1 to 1000. |
| `min_replies` | no | `count - 1`, at least 1 | Replies needed for `expect: success`: an integer from 1 to `count`. One lost packet is tolerated by default (first-packet ARP). Not allowed with `expect: failure` |
| `vrf` | no | `default` | Runs in the VRF (`ip vrf exec` on FRR) or network-instance namespace (`srbase-<name>` on SR Linux) |

- `expect: failure` passes only with 0 replies, and is a post-convergence check.
- `expect: failure` also passes when ping reports the destination unreachable without sending anything: "Network unreachable" (or "Network is unreachable"), "No route to host" or "Destination unreachable" (0.3.1 and later). With no route at all, ping prints one of these and no statistics.
- If ping did not run at all for any other reason (bad source address, missing VRF), the check fails with an error. It never counts as a successful "failure".

```yaml
- type: ping
  node: r1
  source: 192.168.1.1
  target: 192.168.3.1
```

## Failure scenarios

`scenarios:` runs extra checks while something is wrong, then puts it right. Use it to prove the network survives a failure, for example that traffic reroutes when an uplink dies, or that your max-prefix limit and import filters hold when a neighbor misbehaves.

```yaml
scenarios:
  - name: r1-r2 link fails
    link_down: {node: r1, interface: eth1}   # or a list of links
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, protocol: bgp}   # rerouted via r3
      - {type: ping, node: r1, source: 192.168.1.1, target: 192.168.2.1}
      - {type: bgp_session, node: r1, neighbor: 10.0.12.2, state: down}

  - node_isolated: r2          # all of r2's lab links down
    checks:
      - {type: route, node: r1, prefix: 192.168.2.0/24, present: false}

  - name: customer floods us
    inject_routes: {node: ce1, count: 200, from: 10.100.16.0/24}   # ce1 announces 200 extra /24s
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_prefixes, node: up1, neighbor: 10.0.2.1, max: 51}   # the max-prefix limit holds

  - name: peer announces what it does not own
    inject_routes: {node: peer1, prefixes: [10.100.0.0/25, 8.8.8.0/24], as_path: [65400]}
    checks:
      - {type: bgp_prefixes, node: pe2, neighbor: 10.0.4.2, max: 1}   # the import filter holds
      - {type: route, node: ce1, prefix: 10.100.0.0/25, protocol: bgp, present: false}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Label shown before each check (default: generated from the faults) |
| `link_down` | `{node, interface}` or a list of them; no other keys. Interface names as seen inside the node (for example `eth1` on FRR): a Linux interface name of at most 15 letters, digits and `. _ @ -` (checked from 0.3.1). SR Linux links can't be failed yet; fail the FRR or Linux side instead |
| `node_isolated` | A node name, `{node}`, or a list of them: every lab link of that node goes down |
| `inject_routes` | `{node, prefixes}` or `{node, count}` (or a list of them): the node announces extra routes. 0.3.1 and later. See below |
| `checks` | Same check types and keys as the top level. See [scenario timing](#scenario-timing) |

A scenario needs at least one fault and at least one check, and accepts no other keys. Scenarios run after the main checks, one at a time. Links and injected routes are always restored afterwards, even if a check fails, and Netdryrun waits for the network to settle before the next scenario. If the network does not recover, the checks that passed before the scenario are reported as failed `[after <scenario>] recovers: ...` checks, and later scenarios are skipped.

### Scenario timing

A scenario's positive checks ("the route is still there", "ping still works") are already true before the network notices the failure, so Netdryrun makes sure they are never judged on the state from before the fault (0.3.1 and later):

1. Before taking links down, it notes the established BGP sessions that run over them, on both ends of each link (looking through bridges), in the default VRF and the VRFs the scenario's checks use. If that BGP state, or the addresses of the downed interfaces, can't be read, the run stops with exit code `2` naming the node, before any link goes down: "couldn't read it" is never taken for "there are none". A node no driver can read (a Linux host) and a VRF the node doesn't have have no sessions to note.
2. After applying the faults, it waits until every one of those sessions is down **on both ends**: proof that the network saw the fault. The wait is capped at the largest `timeout` of the scenario's checks. If the fault still isn't visible by then, the run stops with exit code `2` and "the fault did not take effect", never a verdict. Without BFD, BGP can take its hold time (up to 180 s) to notice a failure: raise the checks' `timeout`, or lower the hold timers in the lab.
3. It waits the settle delay (`--settle`), so withdrawals propagate beyond the adjacent routers.
4. Positive checks must pass on 2 consecutive samples **and** keep passing for the hold window (`--hold`; a positive check can't set its own `hold`): a redundancy claim is about the whole failure, not one instant. A check that passes at first and then fails within the window fails.
5. Post-convergence checks then wait for the same [BGP gate](#convergence-semantics) as at the top level: every BGP session on their node up, with unchanged prefix counts on 2 consecutive samples, capped at their `timeout`. Sessions over the downed links don't count (the fault took them down), nor do sessions a `bgp_session` check in the scenario or at the top level expects in another state. If another session on the node stays down, the checks fail as **not evaluated**; a session the fault takes down indirectly (for example iBGP between loopbacks whose only path was the downed link) needs a `bgp_session` check with `state: down` in the scenario. Then the checks must hold, as everywhere else. 0.3.1 and later.

When the state was read and no BGP session runs over the downed links (static routing, a link without BGP, iBGP between loopbacks over an IGP), step 2 has nothing to observe; steps 3 to 5 still apply, so give such scenarios a `--settle` that covers the failure detection time. `inject_routes` faults have no step 2: Netdryrun instead waits until the injected prefixes are in the node's own BGP table. That alone doesn't show they reached the node under test; the BGP gate in step 5 does, for post-convergence checks: their node's prefix counts must stop changing first. The limit: a peer with a long advertisement interval (for example eBGP with a 30-second `advertisement-interval`) can hold the routes back for longer than 2 samples 3 seconds apart, so they can still arrive after the gate. Raise `--settle` above the advertisement interval for such labs.

### Injecting routes

New in 0.3.1: Netdryrun 0.3.0 rejects the key as unknown.

`inject_routes` makes a node announce routes it normally doesn't, so you can test what the rest of the network does with them: a customer leaking more-specifics, a peer announcing someone else's prefix, a flood that should trip a max-prefix limit.

| Key | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `node` | yes | The node that announces the routes. It must be an FRR node with `router bgp` in the default VRF |
| `prefixes` | one of | A prefix or list of prefixes, IPv4 or IPv6 |
| `count` | one of | Announce this many consecutive prefixes (1 to 10000), starting at `from` |
| `from` | no | First prefix for `count`; its length is used for all of them. Default `100.64.0.0/24` |
| `as_path` | no | List of AS numbers prepended to the injected routes, so they look learned from those networks |

On the node, Netdryrun adds a blackhole static route and a BGP `network` statement per prefix (with `as_path`, through a route-map named `NDR-INJECT`). It applies them with `vtysh -f` and waits until every prefix is in the node's own BGP table before running the scenario's checks (whose post-convergence checks then wait for the BGP gate on their own node; see [scenario timing](#scenario-timing)). Afterwards it removes exactly what it added and waits until the prefixes are gone. What the node's neighbors do with the routes is up to the policy under test: an outbound filter on the node itself can still stop them.

Limits: only FRR nodes are supported. Any other node is refused before the lab deploys; inject the routes from an FRR neighbor instead. A prefix that is already a `network` statement or a static route on the node is refused, because removing it afterwards would delete real config. IPv6 prefixes need the BGP sessions to carry IPv6 unicast.

## Convergence semantics

Networks need time to converge, and some checks are trivially true before they do. Netdryrun splits checks into two groups.

**Positive checks** (session `established`, prefix count with only `min`, route present, a `bgp_route` best path that exists with no attribute asserted, ping expected to succeed):

- Polled every 3 seconds until they pass on **2 consecutive samples**, or until `timeout` expires.
- A single lucky sample is not enough. If the last sample passed but the streak was too short, the result says "not stable". If the check passed some samples but not consistently, the result says "flapping".

**Post-convergence checks** are the ones that would pass on a network that has not come up yet:

- routes that must be absent (`present: false` on `route` or `bgp_route`)
- best-path attributes (`bgp_route` with any of `communities`, `without_communities`, `as_path`, `as_path_regex`, `local_pref`, `med`, `next_hop`): a best path seen while a slower session is still coming up can be replaced when it arrives
- pings that must fail (`expect: failure`)
- sessions expected in a state other than `established`
- prefix counts with an upper bound (`max` or `exact`), since 0 prefixes satisfies `max: 10` while BGP is still starting

They run in this order:

1. Every positive check has finished.
2. **Every BGP session on the node is up.** Positive checks only prove convergence for the sessions and routes you happened to check, and a leak can arrive later over a session nobody checked. So for each node (and VRF) that carries a post-convergence check, Netdryrun waits until every configured BGP neighbor there is `established`, with unchanged prefix counts, on 2 consecutive samples. Neighbors that a `bgp_session` check expects in another state (for example `state: down`) don't count. The wait is capped at the largest `timeout` of that node's post-convergence checks. If a session there never comes up, those checks fail as **not evaluated**, naming the session: a down session is a finding, as everywhere else. If a session is down on purpose, add a `bgp_session` check with `state: down` for it. (A node that never answers with BGP state, or whose positive checks never got usable state, is not waited for; prefix counts still changing at the cap don't block.) A node that answers with **no BGP neighbors at all** is not converged: that is what a node answers before its BGP config is applied, and a leak can arrive once it is. Netdryrun keeps waiting, up to the cap. If the node still reports no neighbors then and the file says it runs BGP (a `bgp_session`, `bgp_prefixes` or `bgp_route` check on it, or a `route` check with `protocol: bgp`), its post-convergence checks fail as **not evaluated** ("reported no BGP neighbors by the cap"), every sample unready, so a leak guard can't pass on a router whose BGP config never loaded (from 0.3.2; when nothing anywhere gave usable state, the run is inconclusive). A node with no BGP check anywhere in the file may not run BGP at all: its post-convergence checks run anyway, each with a warning in its result ("reported no BGP neighbors for N s; the check was evaluated without BGP convergence"), and the verdict is unchanged. So a node that doesn't run BGP adds one `timeout` of waiting before its post-convergence checks. 0.3.1 and later.
3. A settle delay (`--settle`, default 10 seconds; at least 30 seconds if the file has no positive checks, because nothing else has shown that the network converged). From 0.4, `--settle` and `--hold` stretch to the longest BGP advertisement interval any session in the lab reports, plus 2 seconds: a peer sends at most once per interval, so a route can arrive that late. **On Arista EOS the advertisement delay (`neighbor ... out-delay`) is not read yet** (planned for 0.4.1): if you configure one, raise `--settle` and `--hold` above it, or a leak sent after the windows can pass a negative check.
4. Each one must then hold for the hold window (`--hold` or the check's `hold`, default 10 seconds), sampled every 3 seconds. A violation at any sample fails the check immediately.

### Config that fails to load

A pass only means something if the lab ran the config you wrote. FRR loads its config line by line at boot and skips a line it rejects (a typo, an incomplete command, a command this release doesn't have), so after the checks Netdryrun reads the boot log of every FRR node in the lab: any rejected line makes the run an **error (exit 2)**, naming the node, the line and the reason. A daemon can complain about a line and still apply it (bgpd answers `bgp graceful-restart` with "Failure to communicate" on FRR 10.4.1). So such a line doesn't count when line N of the node's `frr.conf` is that line and that daemon's own running config (`vtysh -d <daemon>`) has it under the same headers at every depth (`router bgp`, VRF, address family, `vni`), at least as many times as the file does, and has the line's whole block as written. A refused header line (`vni 10`, `address-family ...`) always counts. Every other kind of rejection always counts, and so does any line when the running config or `frr.conf` can't be read. A boot log that can't be read is an error too, and so is an FRR node whose log shows no sign of a config load (Netdryrun reads the load FRR's image runs at boot: `frr.conf` through `vtysh -b`, or a daemon reading its own file). Only the current boot counts, so a line fixed and reloaded with a restart no longer does. A node whose driver can't be detected (FRR in an image not named for it) is read when its log shows FRR's rejected lines (an error); otherwise the report says `not verified (no routing driver)`. A `setup:` command that fails (`vtysh -c` exits 1 on a rejected line) stops the run on every platform.

Known limit: **A line FRR warned about but applied can still make the run an error** (fail closed). Only a line a daemon answered with "Failure to communicate" is compared with the running config; a `Warning` line, a line for `mgmtd` (static routes on FRR 10, whose stored config can show a line a daemon then failed to apply) and a line from a daemon's own config file always count. Mitigation: rewrite the line so FRR loads it without a complaint. Fix scheduled: 0.4.1 (a live capture of each kind; was scheduled for 0.4). The comparison also assumes `/etc/frr/frr.conf` is still the file FRR loaded at boot: a lab hook that rewrites it (`write memory`) before the run ends leaves only the check that line N is the reported line. Fix scheduled: 0.4.1 (compare the file's change time with the boot; was scheduled for 0.4).

**Startup config on Arista cEOS, Nokia SR Linux and SONiC** (fixed in 0.4): a line the NOS rejected at boot makes the run an error (exit 2). cEOS skips such a line and loads the rest, like FRR: Netdryrun reads `show startup-config errors` after the checks, and any listed line, or output it can't read, is an error naming the line. SR Linux: a CLI startup config is one commit containerlab applies at deploy, and a line that doesn't parse or a commit that fails fails the deploy; a JSON one SR Linux loads itself and, when it rejects it, runs without it while the deploy succeeds, so Netdryrun reads its log ("Load of startup configuration failed"; a log it can't read is an error). SONiC (docker-sonic-vs) has no startup config: it is configured with `setup:` commands, which stop the run when they exit non-zero; a config file bound into a SONiC node's `/etc`, `/usr` or `/var/lib`, or an inline startup config, is an error. A `setup:` command is checked by its exit code only: SONiC's `config ...` commands and CONFIG_DB writes can exit 0 and fail later, so configure SONiC's routing with `vtysh -c` lines, which fail at once. On a lab Netdryrun didn't deploy (`netdryrun check`), SR Linux and SONiC say `not verified`. **A topology `exec:` command that fails** is an error on every platform: containerlab only logs it and exits 0, and the node runs without what it configured. **Juniper cJunosEvolved (beta): the config load is not verified yet**; the report says `not verified on junos`: add a positive check for what each changed line creates.

Known limit: **Graceful restart on SR Linux, EOS and SONiC** (found by the 0.3.3 cross-platform review): while a peer restarts with graceful restart, its routes stay in the table marked stale until it re-sends them or the stale timer ends, and on these platforms the BGP checks count a stale path as present and best. A route check can pass on a route that is about to go. On FRR, Netdryrun reads the stale flag: a route or `bgp_route` check never passes on a stale path (0.3.3). Mitigation: leave graceful restart off in the lab, or give the checks a `timeout` above the stale timer. Fix scheduled: 0.4.1 (read the stale flag on the other platforms, from a live graceful-restart capture; was scheduled for 0.4).

Known limit: **SR Linux prefix counts** (found by the 0.3.3 cross-platform review, seen on a live SR Linux 26.7.2): a `bgp_prefixes` count on SR Linux includes routes dropped by BGP loop detection, which are not usable, so a `min` or `exact` check can pass with fewer usable prefixes. Mitigation: pair the count with `route` checks for the prefixes that matter. Fix scheduled: 0.4.1 (count usable routes only; was scheduled for 0.4).

Known limit: the gate sees sessions up and prefix counts stable, not routes still in flight. A peer with a long BGP advertisement interval can deliver a route after a post-convergence check was released and held, so a leak guard can pass on a route that hadn't arrived yet. From 0.4, `--settle` and `--hold` stretch automatically to the longest advertisement interval any session reports, plus 2 s (FRR and SONiC per neighbor, SR Linux `minimum-advertisement-interval`), and the run log says so. Still a limit: on Arista EOS a configured `out-delay` is not read (fix scheduled: 0.4.1), so raise `--settle` and `--hold` above it there; a route that crosses several slow peers can take one interval per hop.

Prefix counts with an upper bound start like this (step 4), because counters ramp up and the BGP gate has already waited for stable counts:

- `max` only: no wait. The count must be within `max` from the first sample of the hold window to the last (0 prefixes is within any `max`).
- `exact: N` (N at least 1) and `min` with `max`: first a short wait, up to 30 seconds (or `timeout` if shorter), for the count to reach at least N (or `min`); a count that never gets there fails. Then the full condition (`exact`, or the whole range) must hold on every sample of the hold window, so a count that overshoots fails.
- `exact: 0`: no wait; it must hold like `max: 0`.

`hold` is accepted only on post-convergence checks. A positive check passes after 2 consecutive passing samples, so a `hold` on it would be ignored; that is an error rather than a silent no-op. (Inside a scenario, positive checks do hold for `--hold`; see [scenario timing](#scenario-timing).)

Results are reported in the order the checks appear in the file.

## Drivers

A driver turns device state into a common shape. Netdryrun detects it from the topology:

- `kind: nokia_srlinux` or `kind: srl` uses `srlinux`
- `kind: arista_ceos` or `kind: ceos` uses `eos`
- `kind: juniper_cjunosevolved` or `kind: cjunosevolved` uses `junos` (beta)
- `kind: sonic-vs`, or an image whose name contains `sonic`, uses `sonic`
- an image whose name contains `frr` uses `frr`
- anything else is an error unless you set `nodes.<node>.driver`

| Check | FRR | SR Linux | Arista EOS | SONiC | Juniper cJunosEvolved (beta) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bgp_session` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `bgp_prefixes` (accepted = received minus rejected by policy) | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `route` present / absent | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `bgp_route`: communities (standard, large, well-known), AS path, local preference, MED, next hop, absent | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `ping` success / failure | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Failure scenarios on the node's own links | yes | not yet (fail the FRR/Linux side instead) | yes | yes | not yet (fail the FRR/Linux side instead) |
| `inject_routes` on the node | yes | not yet (inject from an FRR neighbor) | not yet | not yet | not yet |
| Tested on a live lab in CI | yes, on every push | yes, on every push | no: parsers tested against output captured from live labs | no: parsers tested against output captured from live labs | no: parsers tested against output captured from a live lab; needs KVM |

**Received paths count as present on every driver:** a BGP route that lost to a static or local route, or that has an unresolvable next hop, may live only in the BGP table, not the routing table. Every driver reads the BGP table too, so a path received from a neighbor counts as present for `present: false`, valid or not, selected or not. The router's own paths (network statements, redistribution, and on SR Linux its static and interface routes listed in the BGP RIB) don't count as received. Neither does a route the import policy rejected, which FRR and Arista EOS drop and SR Linux and Junos keep, marked (SR Linux: `invalid-reason` `rejected-route`; Junos: hidden, "Rejected by import policy"). An SR Linux path marked invalid for any other reason is an error until the driver reads that reason.

**Errors are never "nothing":** from 0.3.1, a failed command or output a driver doesn't recognize is an error on that sample (the check fails with `error: ...`), never read as "no routes" or "no sessions", which would pass `present: false` or `max`. A VRF that doesn't exist on the node is an error too, on every driver: FRR and SONiC confirm the VRF with `show vrf`, SR Linux reads the network-instance's oper-state, and Arista EOS requires the VRF in the `vrfs` map of its answer. `vrf: all` and other names that mean "every VRF" are refused.

**SONiC:** `docker-sonic-vs` routes with FRR inside the container, so the `sonic` driver reads state through `vtysh` like the FRR driver. The image boots unconfigured; put interface IPs (`config interface ip add ...`) and BGP (`vtysh -c ...`) in `nodes.<node>.setup`. See `examples/sonic-frr`.

**Juniper cJunosEvolved (beta):** free from Juniper for non-production labs, and can't be redistributed: download it yourself and `docker load` it. It boots a VM, so the host needs KVM and about 8 GB of memory per node. Hidden routes count as received, except routes rejected by import policy. See the [Juniper driver page](junos.md) and `examples/junos-frr`.

**Arista EOS:** cEOS-lab is free from arista.com (account required) and can't be redistributed. Download it yourself, then `docker import cEOS-lab-<version>.tar ceos:<version>`, and use `kind: arista_ceos` with that image.

| Driver | Source of state |
|---|---|
| FRR | `vtysh -c "show ... json"`; accepted prefixes from `acceptedPrefixCounter`; `bgp_route` from `show bgp <afi> unicast <prefix> json` |
| SR Linux | `sr_cli --output-format json "info from state ..."`; accepted = `received-routes` minus `rejected-routes`; `bgp_route` from the `bgp-rib` local RIB and its `attr-sets` |
| Arista EOS | `Cli -c "show ... \| json"`; `bgp_route` from `show ip bgp <prefix> vrf <vrf>` (the best path is the `active` one) |
| SONiC | the FRR commands, through `vtysh` inside the container |
| Juniper cJunosEvolved (beta) | `cli -c "show ... \| display json"` over the container's SSH hop to the Junos VM; accepted prefixes = `received-prefix-count` minus the hidden routes rejected by import policy; `route` and `bgp_route` from `show route <prefix> exact table <table> all extensive` (hidden routes included) |

If a driver can't read what a check asks for, the run stops before deploying (exit code `2`) instead of guessing: "`<key>` is not supported on `<driver>`" for a `bgp_route` attribute (today every driver reads every attribute), and "afi evpn is not supported on eos" (or `srlinux`, `junos`) for an EVPN prefix count on Arista EOS, SR Linux or Juniper, and "med: 0 can't be checked on eos: EOS output cannot tell MED 0 from no MED" for `med: 0` on Arista EOS.

Every command and its raw output is kept in the [JSON report](cli.md#json).

## Protocol names

`protocol` on a route check is compared in lower case with the protocol the device reports, after normalization:

| Use | FRR reports | SR Linux reports |
|---|---|---|
| `bgp` | `bgp` | `bgp` |
| `static` | `static` | `static` |
| `connected` | `connected` | `local` |
| `local` | `local` | `host` |
| `ospf` | `ospf` | `ospfv2` |
| `ospf6` | `ospf6` | `ospfv3` |
| `isis` | `isis` | `isis` |

`protocol` must be one of these names (case-insensitive): `bgp`, `connected`, `local`, `static`, `kernel`, `ospf`, `ospf6`, `isis`, `rip`, `ripng`, `aggregate`, `eigrp`, `babel`, `nhrp`, `table`, `sharp`, `pbr`, `openfabric`, `bgp-evpn`, `bgp-vpn`, `dhcp`, `arp-nd`, `gribi`. Any other name is a config error with a suggestion where one is close (`direct` → `connected`, `ospfv3` → `ospf6`); `ebgp` and `ibgp` are refused because drivers report both as `bgp`. Before 0.3.1 an unknown name was passed through, matched nothing, and silently passed `present: false`. The failure detail lists the protocols that were seen.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/reference/cli/

# CLI and reports

```text
netdryrun run      [path] [options]   deploy the lab, run checks, destroy the lab
netdryrun check    [path] [options]   run checks against an already running lab
netdryrun validate [path]             validate netdryrun.yml without running anything
netdryrun record   topology.clab.yml  snapshot a known-good lab into a netdryrun.yml baseline
netdryrun verify   topology.clab.yml  compare the lab before and after a change against a declared intent (0.4, FRR only)
netdryrun mcp                         start the MCP server for AI agents (stdio)
netdryrun feedback                    open a short feedback form on GitHub
netdryrun --version
```

`--debug` (before or after the command: `netdryrun --debug run` or `netdryrun run --debug`) prints the Python traceback of an internal error. Setting `NETDRYRUN_DEBUG=1` does the same.

`path` is `netdryrun.yml` or the folder containing it. Default: the current folder.

`verify` has its own page: [verify](verify.md).

## Commands

### run

Deploys the containerlab topology (`containerlab deploy --reconfigure`), runs every check, writes reports, and destroys the lab (`containerlab destroy --cleanup`). The lab is destroyed even when checks fail, unless you ask to keep it.

`run` refuses to start (exit code `2`) when a lab with the same name is already running: another Netdryrun run of the same lab, a lab deployed by hand, or one kept with `--keep`. Redeploying it would reconfigure the other lab's containers, and destroying it afterwards would pull them out from under whoever is using it. The error names a container and the command to remove the lab: `containerlab destroy -t <topology> --cleanup`. Two runs of the same lab started at the same moment on one host are also refused, by a lock (`another Netdryrun run is already using lab '<name>' on this host`). `check` doesn't deploy, so it runs against the existing lab.

### check

Runs the checks against a lab that is already up, for example one left running with `--keep`. It does not deploy or destroy anything. It fails with an error if any of the lab's containers are not running.

### validate

Loads and validates `netdryrun.yml` and prints the parsed checks. It does not need Docker or containerlab.

From 0.3.1 it also reads the topology (strictly: malformed YAML and duplicate keys are errors) and checks what `run` checks before deploying: every node a check, fault or `setup` names exists; the driver can read every key the checks use (for example no `afi: evpn` on SR Linux, Arista EOS or Juniper); and `inject_routes` names an FRR node. It also checks two things `run` finds out only after deploying: every node a check reads has a driver (detected from its kind and image, or set with `nodes.<node>.driver`), and no `link_down` or `node_isolated` fault targets an SR Linux or cJunosEvolved node. Any of these is an error with exit code `2`. What it can't check without containerlab: whether containerlab accepts the topology itself (a misspelled `kind:`, a missing image).

```text
$ netdryrun validate examples/frr-bgp
OK: examples/frr-bgp/netdryrun.yml (7 checks, lab .../examples/frr-bgp/topology.clab.yml, 3 nodes)
  - [bgp_session] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established
  ...
```

### record

```bash
netdryrun record path/to/topology.clab.yml --deploy
```

Snapshots a known-good lab into a `netdryrun.yml` baseline: every established BGP session, every prefix count and up to 50 BGP routes per node and address family. From 0.3.3 a prefix count is a range: today's count as `min`, and `max` with 20% headroom (at least 2) for normal growth, which still catches a leak that multiplies the count; a neighbor that sends nothing stays `exact: 0`. When a node has more BGP routes than are recorded, the file starts with an `# INCOMPLETE BASELINE` line naming the node and the count, and the same line is printed on stderr: a change to an unrecorded route goes unnoticed, so add checks for the routes that matter. From 0.4 it covers every active VRF on FRR and SONiC, each check with its `vrf:`; on SR Linux and Arista EOS it records the default VRF only and says so in a warning (add checks for other VRFs by hand). Commit it, and every later change is tested against today's behavior. Review the file before committing: remove what is allowed to change, and add negative checks for what must never happen.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out FILE` | Where to write (default: `netdryrun.yml` next to the topology) |
| `--deploy` | Deploy the lab first and destroy it afterwards (otherwise the lab must be running) |
| `--wait SECONDS` | With `--deploy`: time for BGP to converge before recording (default 45) |
| `--exact-prefixes` | Pin prefix counts exactly (0.3.2 and earlier did this by default) |
| `--min-prefixes` | Record prefix counts as minimums only |
| `--no-guards` | Leave out the standard [guards](../recipes.md#guard-recipes), which `record` writes by default from 0.3.3: on each BGP node, no default route via BGP (`0.0.0.0/0`, and `::/0` with IPv6 BGP) and no link subnet of the topology via BGP, each as a `route` check with `present: false`. Each guard is first run on the recording lab: one the lab already fails (a default the node learns or merely receives via BGP from upstream, say) is left out, and a comment in the file says why. They are on by default because a prefix-count range has room for one leaked default route |
| `--no-routes` | Don't record individual routes |
| `--attributes` | Also record a `bgp_route` check per BGP route, pinning its best path's AS path, local preference and communities (not MED or next hop, which follow the topology) |
| `--force` | Overwrite an existing file |

### feedback

Opens a short feedback form on GitHub in your browser, prefilled with your Netdryrun version and platform. Nothing is sent until you submit the form.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--print-only` | Print the form's URL instead of opening a browser |

## Options

`run` and `check`:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--json FILE` | | Write the full evidence report as JSON |
| `--markdown FILE` | | Write a Markdown summary (for PR comments) |
| `--junit FILE` | | Write JUnit XML (for CI test reporting) |
| `--verdict FILE` | | Write the agent result as JSON: status, verdict, failures and the sha256 of every file tested, the shape the MCP tools return (from 0.3.3) |
