### Nondeterministic cases (not scored)

Same build, same machine, same case, different verdicts: the verdict follows a race in the lab, not the change. These cases are left out of every score above and listed here with every Netdryrun verdict seen. The case files and expected verdicts are unchanged; the list is in `corpus/v2/NONDETERMINISTIC.yml`.

- **`18-aggregate-discard-route-removed` Discard route for our aggregate deleted as unused** (expected unsafe). With the discard route for 192.0.2.0/24 deleted, FRR's BGP import check (enabled: the path shows "inaccessible, import-check enabled") sometimes withholds the aggregate and sometimes announces it. Withheld, the upstream and the peer lose it and the intent checks (I2, I5) fail; announced, they pass, and the harm left is the routing loop for unused addresses in the aggregate, which no check probes. Same build, same machine, same case: different verdicts. Netdryrun verdicts: 2026-10-27, first v2 run, development build before 0.3.1: **safe**; 2026-10-27, 0.3.1 release gate rerun (the committed results.json): **unsafe**; 2026-10-29, 0.3.3 release gate, build ada4dd0: **safe**; 2026-10-29, rerun 1 of 3, build ada4dd0: **unsafe**; 2026-10-29, rerun 2 of 3, build ada4dd0: **unsafe**; 2026-10-29, rerun 3 of 3, build ada4dd0: **safe**.

### Netdryrun's losses

- **`04-redundant-aggregate-typo` Aggregate added on pe2 for redundancy, mistyped as 192.0.12.0/24** (false pass). Expected to be missed. I7 only spot-checks a few well-known prefixes, and nothing bounds what the customer receives.

### Findings after the run

These findings came after the v2 run. The table above is left exactly as pre-registered in commit `322cc4e`; nothing in [`corpus/v2/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/corpus/v2/cases) was edited.

**Run provenance.** `results.json` records the commit as `unknown`: the run used git inside WSL on a Windows git worktree, and that git could not read the worktree. The run started at 04:02:42 UTC, 16 seconds after the pre-registration commit `322cc4e`. `src/` and `corpus/run.py` were not changed during the run. The renderer, the docs and the unit tests were edited during the run, and none of them affect verdicts.

**Case 04 is a real miss, as predicted.** pe2 announced the mistyped 192.0.12.0/24 to pe1 and on to the customer, and no check looked for it. I7 only spot-checks a few well-known prefixes, and nothing bounds what the customer receives. Catching this class needs a check that the customer receives only routes from known origins, or only expected prefixes from our own AS. No such check type exists yet.

**Case 18 is a real miss.** ~~With the discard route deleted, FRR (traditional defaults, no `bgp network import-check`) kept announcing 192.0.2.0/24, so I2 passed.~~ *Corrected 2026-10-29: in this run FRR kept announcing 192.0.2.0/24, so I2 passed. But FRR's import check is enabled in this lab, and whether it withholds the aggregate is a race: see the last paragraph.* The harm is the routing loop for unused addresses inside the aggregate, which no check probes. A `ping` with `expect: failure` to an unused address in 192.0.2.0/24 from the upstream would not show the loop either, because ping fails both with and without it. Catching it needs a path or traceroute check (TTL exceeded versus a clean discard).

**Ping only's catch of case 14 is partly a lab artifact.** In the lab, the customer's BGP default is not active, because containerlab's management default route outranks it (the spec checks the default with `active: false` for this reason). Once the customer lost its specific routes, its pings had no path at all. A real customer with a working default would still ping, and the ping baseline would pass the change. The result stays as measured.

**Rerun on the released 0.3.1 (2026-10-27, by the release gate):** every verdict matches the first run except case 18 (`18-aggregate-discard-route-removed`). The development build approved it; 0.3.1 rejects it, which is the pre-registered expected verdict, because the upstream and the peer no longer receive the aggregate (checks I2 and I5 fail). ~~0.3.1 changed how routes are read (received paths count, errors are never read as "no routes"), and this case was one of v2's two misses. Netdryrun is now 17/18 on v2.~~ *Corrected 2026-10-29: 0.3.1 did not cause the flip, and 17/18 overstated the result: see the next paragraph.* The cases and the expected verdicts are unchanged.

**Case 18 is nondeterministic in this lab (found 2026-10-29 by the 0.3.3 release gate).** The 0.3.3 gate's rerun approved it again. Three more runs of the same build on the same machine gave unsafe, unsafe, safe. FRR's BGP import check is enabled (the path reads "inaccessible, import-check enabled"), and with the discard route gone it sometimes withholds the aggregate and sometimes announces it. The verdict follows that race, not Netdryrun's code. From 0.3.3 the case is listed in `NONDETERMINISTIC.yml` with every verdict seen. It is left out of the score: v2 is **16 of 17 deterministic cases correct**. The release gate runs it three times, records the verdicts and never blocks on them; a verdict change on any other case still blocks a release. A replacement with the same intent and the race removed goes into a later corpus version, its expected verdict committed before it runs. This case file and its expected verdict are not edited.

Source: https://netdryrun.com/how-its-built/

# How Netdryrun is built and verified

A tool that approves network changes has to earn trust with evidence, not claims. Most of this page links to something you can inspect or rerun yourself: the test corpus, the CI runs, the commit history and the release pipeline. Where a claim can't be checked yet, the page says so.

## At a glance

| | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Accuracy on realistic BGP changes | Verdict Corpus v1: **24/30** (ping only 20/30, sessions up 15/30). v2: **16 of 17** deterministic cases (ping only 9/17, sessions up 7/17); case 18 is nondeterministic in this lab and not scored. Both ran on Netdryrun 0.3.1 (the release gate reruns them for every release). [Results](corpus.md) |
| Expected verdicts fixed before any run | Committed first, never edited: [`b4df0b0`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/b4df0b0) (v1), [`322cc4e`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/322cc4e) (v2) |
| Results you can rerun | One command locally (`python corpus/run.py`, `--corpus v2` for v2). The [Reproduce corpus](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/reproduce-corpus.yml) workflow reruns v1 from your own fork; it has not been run on GitHub yet |
| Real labs on every change | FRR and Nokia SR Linux labs boot in CI on every push and pull request ([runs](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/actions/workflows/ci.yml)) |
| What users install is tested too | The released Action and the PyPI package, on every push and weekly ([`published-action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/published-action.yml)) |
| Supply chain | PyPI Trusted Publishing, CodeQL, OpenSSF Scorecard, every Action pinned to a commit |
| Losses | Published next to the wins, never removed |

## Engineering process

Every change goes through the same CI tests and lab runs, and every release through the release gate described below. The [commit history](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commits/main) records every change.

## Pre-registered accuracy testing

The [Verdict Corpus](corpus.md) measures Netdryrun on realistic BGP changes, each labelled harmful or safe in advance, and compares it with two common checks: "ping still works" and "all BGP sessions are up".

- **Verdicts are committed before anything runs.** v1: all 30 cases with their expected verdicts in [`b4df0b0`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/b4df0b0), results later in [`7576298`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/7576298). v2: 18 new cases in [`322cc4e`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/322cc4e), results later in [`669b30f`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/669b30f). No case was edited after a run ([history of `corpus/cases/`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commits/main/corpus/cases)).
- **The tool was run on the corpus during development, and changed before the published runs.** During 0.2.0 development, runs against the v1 cases found a bug (a change that broke a baseline check ended a scenario run as `error`) and showed that the new polling made the corpus 2 to 3 times faster; both are in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). The expected verdicts were not changed; the v1 intent spec changed by one comment line.
- **Both published runs were rerun on the released 0.3.1** by the release gate (commit `08059de`, code identical to the v0.3.1 tag). The first runs used pre-release builds: v1 on commit `ec23379` (it called itself 0.2.0, before the tagged 0.2.0), v2 on a development build that recorded no commit. On 0.3.1 every v1 verdict is the same; v2 changed on case 18 (now rejected, as expected), recorded in [AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/AMENDMENTS.md).
- **v2 is a harder test, not a friendlier one.** Its cases target the kinds of change v1 missed. It was written after seeing v1's results, which is a limitation to keep in mind.
- **Everything reruns.** The runner ([`corpus/run.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/run.py)), every case and the raw output ([`results.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/results/results.json)) are public. `python corpus/run.py` reruns v1 and `--corpus v2` reruns v2, with the code you have checked out (so a different verdict can come from a code change, not only from noise). The GitHub workflow reruns v1 the same way on a hosted runner and lists any verdict that differs; it has not been run on GitHub yet, and it does not cover v2.
- **Limit of this evidence:** git commit dates come from the author's machine. The history proves the order of the commits and that the cases were not changed; it is not an independent timestamp.

## Every miss, and what it changed

A test you always pass tells you nothing. Netdryrun's misses stay in the published results, at the same size as its catches, and each one has driven a specific improvement.


**Verdict Corpus v1: wrong on 6 of 30 cases.** It approved 5 harmful changes and blocked 1 safe one ([RESULTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/RESULTS.md)).


**Verdict Corpus v2: wrong on 1 of 18 cases on 0.3.1**, a harmful change approved. The first run, on a development build, was wrong on 2 ([v2 results](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/v2/RESULTS.md)).

| Case | Outcome | Root cause | What changed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 [06](corpus/06-customer-adds-prefix.md): customer announces a second allowed /24 | Blocked a safe change | The intent spec pinned exactly 2 prefixes towards the upstream and peer, so normal customer growth looked like a leak | v2 checks a range (2 to 51 prefixes); the growth cases 07 and 08 pass | Fixed |
| v1 [12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md): send-community removed on iBGP | Approved | **Our label was wrong.** On FRR, communities are sent by default, so the change is a no-op ([AMENDMENTS.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/corpus/AMENDMENTS.md), with a reproduction script) | Scored as a loss anyway, never corrected in our favour. v2 case 09 tests the corrected expectation and case 10 the truly harmful variant; both judged correctly | Label error |
| v1 [18](corpus/18-redistribute-connected.md): redistribute connected on pe1 | Approved | Spec gap: nothing checked for infrastructure routes leaving the AS | New intent I6: no link or loopback routes at the customer, upstream or peer. v2 case 02 (the same mistake on pe2) caught | Fixed |
| v1 [23](corpus/23-fat-finger-third-party-origin.md): pe1 originates 8.8.8.0/24 | Approved | Spec gap: nothing checked for third-party space | New intent I7, a sentinel list of well-known prefixes. v2 case 03 caught | Partly fixed (see v2 04) |
| v1 [21](corpus/21-customer-max-prefix-removed.md): customer max-prefix removed | Approved | Latent risk, invisible until the customer misbehaves | New `inject_routes` failure scenario: the customer floods 200 prefixes. v2 cases 05 and 11 caught | Fixed (the scenario ships in 0.3.1) |
| v1 [30](corpus/30-peer-import-filter-removed.md): peer inbound filter replaced with permit-all | Approved | Latent risk, invisible until the peer misbehaves | The same scenario type, with the peer announcing routes it does not own. v2 case 06 caught | Fixed (the scenario ships in 0.3.1) |
| v2 04: redundant aggregate mistyped as 192.0.12.0/24 | Approved | I7 checks only a few well-known prefixes; nothing bounds what the customer receives | Predicted as a likely miss in the case file before the run | Open |
| v2 18: discard route for the aggregate deleted | Approved on the development build; **rejected on 0.3.1** | Causes a routing loop for unused addresses inside the aggregate; no check sends traffic there | 0.3.1 reads received paths and never reads an error as "no routes": the upstream and the peer no longer receive the aggregate, so checks I2 and I5 fail. The loop itself is still not probed; a path or traceroute check would show it | Caught on 0.3.1 (not by probing the loop) |

Two caveats apply. v2 was written after seeing v1's misses, so its improvements are measured on cases designed by the same team. And the corpus runs on FRR only, with one topology.

## Continuous integration with live labs

Every push to `main` and every pull request runs [`ci.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml) ([runs](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/actions/workflows/ci.yml)): unit tests on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, plus three jobs that boot real containerlab labs.

- **`e2e`** runs the GitHub Action on [`examples/frr-bgp`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp) and [`examples/srl-frr`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-frr) (FRR and Nokia SR Linux). Both must pass.
- **`catches-bad-change`** runs [`examples/frr-bgp-broken`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken), a change that leaks a default route. The job succeeds only if Netdryrun rejects it.
- **`agent-demo`** replays [`examples/agent-demo`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/agent-demo): a route-leaking change must fail on exactly the leak guards, and the proper fix must pass.

A second workflow, [`published-action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/published-action.yml), tests what users install rather than the code on `main`: the released Action by its tag (it must pass a good change and reject a bad one), and `pip install` and `uvx` from PyPI on every supported Python version, including an MCP handshake.

SONiC and Arista EOS are not in CI yet (cEOS is an image each user downloads from Arista). Their unit tests parse output captured from real lab runs ([`tests/fixtures`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/tests/fixtures)).

Every release also goes through a seven-layer release gate, from linting and mutation testing of the verdict logic to chaos runs on the built package, described in [RELEASING.md](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/RELEASING.md); from the next release on, each release's results are committed in `releases/<version>/GATE.md`.

## Performance on a 20-node fabric

On a 20-node leaf-spine fabric (4 spines, 16 leaves, FRR, 64 links), `netdryrun record` produced 560 checks in 11 seconds, and a full `netdryrun run` (deploy, convergence, all checks, destroy) took 65 seconds. A deliberately broken change failed exactly the 83 checks it should have. Full numbers, memory use and limits are in the [FAQ](faq.md#a-20-node-lab). These come from one-off runs on the maintainer's machine; the topology and the reports are not published yet, so you can't check them the way you can check the corpus.

## Cross-model review (not a human audit)

Before releases 0.1.0 and 0.2.0, the code was also reviewed by AI models from other vendors (OpenAI GPT and xAI Grok); 0.3.0 was not. Separate agent sessions that start without the author's context also review changes. These review outputs are not published. Fixes from these reviews: [`ec23379`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/ec23379) (v0.2.0), [`6495759`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/6495759) (agent demo) and [`90fe0ae`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/90fe0ae): a security review of the MCP server, the GitHub Action and every path where lab output reaches a shell, a device CLI or a PR comment, with 7 findings, each fixed with a regression test.

These reviewers are AI models, not human auditors. No independent human security audit has been done yet. Report vulnerabilities through the [security policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/security/policy).

## Defects found by our own testing

Each was found by running Netdryrun against live labs or the corpus, and is recorded in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

- **False passes on SR Linux and Arista (fixed):** a leaked route that was received but not installed was invisible, so a `present: false` check passed when it should have failed. Fixed in [`77f43d6`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/77f43d6), with regression tests on captured output ([`test_drivers.py`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/tests/test_drivers.py)).
- **Wrong status after a failure scenario (fixed):** a change that broke a baseline check ended as `error` instead of `failed`. Found with [`scripts/pack_verify.sh`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/scripts/pack_verify.sh); fixed in [`f6ea560`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/commit/f6ea560).
- **PR comments over GitHub's size limit on large labs (fixed):** found by the 20-node scale test. From 0.3.1, the comment is cut to fit GitHub's limit, failures first, and says how many checks it left out; the JSON and JUnit reports keep every check.
- **A mislabeled corpus case:** [case 12](corpus/12-ibgp-send-community-dropped.md), above.

## Supply-chain security

- **Releases** are published to PyPI with Trusted Publishing, so no tokens are stored ([`release.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml)). A release fails if the tag and the package version differ.
- **OpenSSF Scorecard** rates the repository's practices weekly and on every push ([current score](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun)), including the checks where it scores low today; the viewer lists each one.
- **CodeQL** scans the Python code and the workflows ([`codeql.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/.github/workflows/codeql.yml)).
- **Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit**, in the workflows and in [`action.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/action.yml). Dependabot keeps the pins current.

## What we do not claim

- **Not production safety.** A pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab running open-source or lab images of network operating systems. It does not prove the change is safe on your network ([what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove)).
- **Not Internet scale.** The largest measured lab has 20 nodes and small routing tables. Nothing here is tested with full Internet tables or hundreds of peers.
- **Not vendor parity.** FRR, SR Linux, SONiC and cEOS behave differently from each other and from hardware routers. The corpus runs only on FRR, with one topology and one intent spec per version, all written by the Netdryrun maintainers.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/batfish/

# Batfish, then Netdryrun

[Batfish](https://batfish.org) and Netdryrun™ answer different questions. Batfish reads configs and models the network's routing and forwarding: nothing has to boot, and in the runs below its analysis took 2 to 6 seconds once the Batfish service was running. Netdryrun boots the configs in a containerlab lab and checks what the routing software really does. Run Batfish first on every commit, and boot the lab only when it passes.

This page reports one measured run of that pipeline: four versions of a small FRR network, each tested by both stages. The code is in [`examples/batfish-pipeline`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/batfish-pipeline).

## The pipeline

The network is the FRR triangle from [`examples/frr-bgp`](examples.md#frr-bgp): three routers, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP.

1. **Batfish** (`batfish_check.py`, 8 checks): every config parses with no parse warnings, no undefined references, all six BGP sessions establish, r1's best paths to the two other LANs, no router learns a default route, a traceroute from r1's LAN to r2's LAN, and the best path after the r1-r2 link fails (a forked snapshot with the interface deactivated).
2. **Netdryrun** (`netdryrun.yml`, 10 checks): r1's two BGP sessions, the prefix count from r2, the route to r2's LAN and its best path, a ping, no default route on r1 or r3, and the same link failure.

The two stages check the same intent with two differences: Batfish checks for a default route on all three routers, while the lab checks r1 and r3 (r2 is the router that would send it), and the lab adds a prefix count and a ping.

```yaml title="examples/batfish-pipeline/github-workflow.yml"
# Example workflow: copy to .github/workflows/ in your repository and adapt the paths.
# Job 1 runs Batfish on every push; nothing boots. Job 2 boots the lab with Netdryrun, only if
# Batfish passed. Not run by this repository's CI.
name: network change gate

on:
  push:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  batfish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    services:
      batfish:
        image: batfish/batfish:2026.08.27.3685
        ports: ["9996:9996", "9997:9997"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install pybatfish==2026.9.17.3748
      - name: Analyse the configs   # waits up to 60 s for the Batfish service to answer
        run: python examples/batfish-pipeline/batfish_check.py examples/batfish-pipeline/configs

  netdryrun:
    needs: batfish   # boot the lab only if Batfish passed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0
        with:
          path: examples/batfish-pipeline
```

The workflow is an example to copy: this repository's CI does not run it, and it has not been timed on GitHub's runners. On top of the analysis, the Batfish job pays for pulling the `batfish/batfish` image (712 MB; `docker pull` took 15 s on the test machine), installing pybatfish (14 s there, the first command of the example's run steps) and starting the service. The measurements below come from the equivalent local script, `pipeline.sh`.

## Results

Measured on 2026-10-27 from a fresh clone of commit f368194 (later commits change only documentation), following the example's [README](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/batfish-pipeline#run-it) word for word, on WSL2 (20 cores, 16 GB) with images already pulled: `batfish/batfish:2026.08.27.3685`, pybatfish 2026.9.17.3748, Netdryrun 0.3.0 from PyPI, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR 10.4.1. The Batfish service was already running. The Batfish stage includes loading the snapshot; the lab stage includes deploying and destroying the lab. Each change below replaces r2's config; the last column is the command that reproduces the row.

| Change to r2 | Batfish | Netdryrun lab | Who caught it | Reproduce |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| None (baseline) | pass, 6 s | pass, 66 s | Both pass | `pipeline.sh` |
| Adds `default-originate` toward r1 | **fail**, 3 s | **fail**, 68 s (2 of 10) | Both; Batfish first | `BOTH=1 pipeline.sh default-leak` |
| Route-map name typo (`ALLOW-AL`) toward r1 | **fail**, 2 s | **fail**, 179 s (2 of 10) | Both; Batfish first, but its route model predicts the wrong outcome | `BOTH=1 pipeline.sh route-map-typo` |
| Switches to `frr defaults traditional` and drops the "allow all" route-maps | pass, 3 s | **fail**, 265 s (6 of 10) | **Only the lab** | `BOTH=1 pipeline.sh no-policy` |

### Caught by Batfish first: a leaked default route

r2 starts sending r1 a default route. In a 3-second run, Batfish reports that r1 learns `0.0.0.0/0` from r2 and passes it on to r3. The lab finds the same leak on r1 and r3 after about a minute. There FRR picks the route as its BGP best path and passes it on, but does not install it as the router's route to 0.0.0.0/0; Netdryrun reports it as "present via bgp (not selected)" and fails the check anyway. Stopping at the Batfish stage saves the lab run.

The route-map typo is also caught first: Batfish's `undefinedReferences` question names the missing `ALLOW-AL` and where it is used, `r2.conf line 20`. (`batfish_check.py` maps lines in the wrapped files it gives Batfish back to the original `frr.conf`.) Its routing model, though, still predicts that r1 uses the direct path to r2. FRR denies everything through a route-map that does not exist, so in the lab r1 receives nothing from r2 and reaches r2's LAN through r3. Ping still works; only the best-path check and the prefix count fail. The gate would fail in both stages, but only the lab shows what the network would really do.

### Seen only by the lab: an FRR default

According to the [FRR documentation](https://docs.frrouting.org/en/latest/bgp.html#clicmd-bgp-ebgp-requires-policy), `bgp ebgp-requires-policy` is on by default under the `traditional` profile and off under `datacenter`. An eBGP neighbor with no inbound and outbound policy then receives nothing and sends nothing, but the session still comes up. In the lab, r2 shows `(Policy) (Policy)` for both neighbors and 0 prefixes each way, and 6 of the 10 checks fail: r2's LAN is unreachable from r1, even after the link-failure scenario.

Batfish passed this change. It accepted `frr defaults traditional` without modelling what that profile implies, and predicted every route as before. When `bgp ebgp-requires-policy` is written out explicitly, Batfish reports it as an unrecognized line rather than applying it (Batfish 2026.08.27.3685; the commands are in the example's [README](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/batfish-pipeline#reproduce-the-findings)).

### Where they agreed

For the r1-r2 link failure, Batfish's forked snapshot predicted the same failover path (AS path `65003 65002` through r3) that the lab measured. In a topology this small, failover did not show any convergence behavior that the model missed.

## What Batfish does that this test does not show

This test uses a small part of Batfish. It also tests route maps and other routing policies against every route they could match, analyses ACLs and firewall rules, searches every packet that could match a rule rather than the few a ping sends, finds forwarding loops, compares two snapshots (for example before and after a change, or with links or nodes failed) to report which flows change, and supports many vendors whose software cannot run in a container. Its authors report analysing networks with thousands of nodes within minutes ([SIGCOMM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866)), far more than a lab can boot. See its [list of questions](https://batfish.readthedocs.io/en/latest/questions.html). None of that needs a lab, and Netdryrun does none of it.

## How well Batfish parses FRR

Batfish reads FRR configs as part of its Cumulus Linux and SONiC support. In this test its FRR support was partial, and the way we fed it configs mattered:" (scopes "partial" to what we measured

- **A bare `frr.conf` is detected as Cisco IOS.** On these configs the status was `PARTIALLY_UNRECOGNIZED`: the `frr defaults` line was not recognized, and interfaces were renamed (`eth1` became `Ethernet1`). The BGP answers happened to be right, but FRR syntax was being read with IOS semantics.
- **Cumulus Linux layout.** Wrapped in the "Cumulus concatenated" layout (a hostname line, an interfaces section, a `ports.conf` marker, then `frr.conf`), the same three configs parse as `CUMULUS_CONCATENATED` with status `PASSED`, no warnings, and the lab's interface names. `batfish_check.py` does this wrapping.
- **SONiC layout.** Next to a `config_db.json` with the hostname and interface addresses, the unchanged `frr.conf` files also parse as `SONIC` with status `PASSED` and no warnings. Batfish predicted the same routes as through the Cumulus path, for the baseline and for the `traditional` change.
- **Not every FRR command or default was supported in this test.** In this test, the defaults profile is accepted but not modelled, and `bgp ebgp-requires-policy` is not recognized at all. Make the gate fail on any file that does not parse cleanly or has a parse warning (`fileParseStatus`, `parseWarning`), as the example script does.

The commands that reproduce these findings, and the `(Policy)` output from FRR, are in the example's [README](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/batfish-pipeline#reproduce-the-findings).

These findings cover only BGP with route-maps on three FRR routers. Batfish's support for other vendors (Cisco, Juniper, Arista, Palo Alto and more) is much broader and is not tested here.

## Related research

A HotNets 2025 paper from Google and UC Berkeley, [Towards Accessible Model-Free Verification](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772356.3772380) (Krentsel et al.), joins the two ideas in one system: it boots real router images in the Kubernetes Network Emulator, extracts the converged data plane, and runs Batfish's existing questions on it. The authors report that this caught changes Batfish could not parse and found bugs in Batfish's model. This page keeps the two as separate stages, with the configs as the only shared input.

## Takeaways

- Put Batfish first. It needs no lab, it failed the two changes it caught in 2 to 3 seconds of analysis, and it pointed at the cause: the file and line of the route-map typo, the routers that learn the leaked default.
- Keep the lab stage. The change that passed Batfish broke every route through r2, because of a vendor default that the model, in the version we tested, did not apply.
- Watch for disagreements, not only for failures. On the route-map typo, both stages failed, but Batfish's prediction of the outcome was wrong.

See also [When to use what](when-to-use-what.md) for how Batfish, pyATS/Genie, containerlab and Netdryrun compare.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/when-to-use-what/

# When to use what

Several good open-source tools help you test network changes. They answer different questions and work well together. This page tries to describe each one fairly; if something here is wrong or out of date, please [open an issue](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/issues).

## The short version

| Tool | Best at | Runs routers? |
|---|---|---|
| [Batfish](https://batfish.org) | Modelling a network from the configs of many vendors, without booting anything: reachability and traceroute, ACLs and firewall rules, routes and routing policy, failure impact, differences between two snapshots | No, it models them |
| [pyATS / Genie](https://developer.cisco.com/pyats/) | A full Python test framework with a large library of device parsers, for testing labs and real (including production) devices, with state snapshots and diffs | Works against any reachable device |
| [containerlab](https://containerlab.dev) | Running container-based network labs from a YAML topology, for many network operating systems | Yes, it is the lab |
| Your own scripts | Exactly the checks your team needs, around a lab you already run, with no new dependency | Yes, through containerlab |
| Netdryrun™ | Declarative, convergence-aware checks on a containerlab lab, packaged for CI with a pass/fail verdict and evidence | Yes, through containerlab |

## Batfish

Batfish parses device configs and uses a model of the control plane (routing protocols such as BGP) to compute the data plane that the configs would produce, then answers questions about it ([Batfish team, SIGCOMM 2023](https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866)). It needs only the configs, not access to devices ([README](https://github.com/batfish/batfish)). Its authors report analysing networks with thousands of nodes within minutes, and it reads configs from many router, firewall and cloud vendors. Its [questions](https://batfish.readthedocs.io/en/latest/questions.html) cover traceroute and reachability over every matching flow, routing tables and BGP sessions, route-map and ACL behavior, and differences between two snapshots, including a copy of the network with chosen links or nodes failed ([failure analysis](https://batfish.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/linked/analyzing-the-impact-of-failures-and-letting-loose-a-chaos-monkey.html)). A question such as "can any host in this subnet reach that server?" covers every packet, which a ping cannot.

Use it on every commit, before a lab boots, especially for ACLs, firewall policy, failure impact and configs from vendors that cannot run in containers.

A model is not the running software. Batfish computes the converged result, not the path the routers take to it, and where the model and the implementation differ (an unmodelled default, a vendor bug), its answer follows the model. A [HotNets 2025 paper from Google and UC Berkeley](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772356.3772380) makes the same point and prototypes "model-free verification": boot real router images in an emulator, extract the converged data plane, and run Batfish's queries on it. That is where a lab helps; our [Batfish page](batfish.md) shows one FRR default the model missed.

## pyATS / Genie

pyATS is a mature Python test framework from Cisco, and Genie adds a large library of parsers and models that turn CLI output into structured data. It can learn the state of a device, take before and after snapshots, and diff them. It works against lab devices and real ones.

Use it when you need deep, programmable testing, broad parser coverage (especially for Cisco platforms), or pre- and post-change checks on production devices.

Netdryrun is narrower: a YAML file and a GitHub Action, with no test code to write, and it only runs against labs. If you already have pyATS tests, keep them.

## containerlab

containerlab runs network labs from a YAML topology: container-native network operating systems (such as Nokia SR Linux, Arista cEOS, Juniper cRPD, FRR) and, through vrnetlab, many VM-based ones. It handles wiring, management addresses and lifecycle.

Use it whenever you want a real lab on a laptop or a CI runner. Netdryrun does not replace it; Netdryrun drives it.

## Your own scripts around containerlab

Many teams already run containerlab in CI with a script that deploys the lab, sleeps, runs a few `show` commands or pings, and tears down. That is free, flexible, and needs no new tool. If your checks are few and your lab rarely changes, keep it.

Scripts tend to get harder in the same places, and those are what Netdryrun packages:

- **Timing.** A fixed `sleep` either wastes minutes or fails while BGP is still converging. Netdryrun polls until each check passes twice in a row, and runs "must never happen" checks only after convergence, for a hold window.
- **Routes that hide.** A leaked route that was received but not selected doesn't show in the main routing table output on every network OS. Netdryrun's drivers read where each one keeps it (FRR, SR Linux, SONiC, cEOS).
- **Evidence.** One verdict, an exit code, JUnit, a PR comment, and a JSON file with every command and its raw output, instead of a log to read.
- **Scenarios and agents.** Link-down and node-isolation scenarios with recovery checks, and an MCP server so an AI agent can run the same checks.

The two mix well: keep a script for anything Netdryrun doesn't check, and call `netdryrun check` from it for the rest.

## Netdryrun

Netdryrun adds a test layer on top of a containerlab lab:

- positive checks wait for convergence and must pass twice in a row
- negative checks (absent routes, failing pings, prefix upper bounds) run only after convergence and must hold
- a route that was received but not selected counts as present
- every run produces one pass/fail result, a CI-friendly exit code, and a JSON evidence file


Version 0.4.0 has drivers for FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista EOS (bring your own cEOS image) and Juniper cJunosEvolved (beta), and its checks cover BGP sessions, prefix counts, routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, with link-down, node-isolation and route-injection (FRR only) failure scenarios.

It does not do static analysis, build labs for you, or test production devices.

## How they combine

A reasonable pipeline uses more than one:

1. **Batfish** on every commit, to analyse the configs before anything boots.
2. A **containerlab** topology that mirrors the change.
3. **Netdryrun** in CI to boot that lab, wait for convergence, and gate the merge on runtime behavior.
4. **pyATS / Genie** (or similar) for pre- and post-change checks on the production devices during the change window.

None of these steps proves the change is safe on its own. Each one removes a different class of mistakes.

[Batfish, then Netdryrun](batfish.md) shows steps 1 and 3 together on a small FRR network, with measured times. In that test, Batfish caught two of three bad changes in seconds, before any lab booted; the third depended on an FRR default that only the running routers showed.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/news/

Subscribe with the [RSS feed](https://netdryrun.com/news/feed.xml). Longer write-up: [Ping and 'BGP up' passed. The route leak was still there.](../posts/ping-missed-the-leak.md)

Source: https://netdryrun.com/posts/ping-missed-the-leak/

# Ping and "BGP up" passed. The route leak was still there.

*2026-10-28 · Netdryrun™ 0.3.1, containerlab 0.81.1, FRR 10.4.1*

A one-line change makes a router send its neighbor a default route. After the change, both BGP sessions are established and the ping between the LANs answers. A test made of those checks reports a pass. The leaked default is in the neighbor's routing table anyway, received but not selected, waiting for the day the route it loses to goes away.

This post walks through that case with the bundled [`frr-bgp-broken`](../examples.md#frr-bgp-broken) example: the lab, the change, the commands, the evidence, and what a lab run like this can and can't tell you. Everything quoted is real output from the runs named next to it.

## The lab and the change

Three FRR routers in a triangle, each in its own AS, each announcing one LAN over eBGP: r1 (AS 65001, `192.168.1.0/24`), r2 (AS 65002, `192.168.2.0/24`) and r3 (AS 65003, `192.168.3.0/24`). The example is the [`frr-bgp`](../examples.md#frr-bgp) lab with one change in r2's config, [`r2-bad.conf`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken/r2-bad.conf):

```text title="r2-bad.conf"
router bgp 65002
 ...
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 192.168.2.0/24
  ! The bad change: someone added default-originate toward r1
  neighbor 10.0.12.1 default-originate
```

`default-originate` makes r2 announce `0.0.0.0/0` to r1 whether or not r2 has a default route itself. Toward a customer that is sometimes intended. Toward a peer, or a router that has its own way out, it offers to carry all traffic that has no more specific route.

## The checks

The example's [`netdryrun.yml`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/examples/frr-bgp-broken/netdryrun.yml) has six checks, all on r1: both BGP sessions established, between 1 and 10 prefixes from r2, a route to r3's LAN, a ping from r1's LAN to r3's, and one negative check:

```yaml
- type: route        # nothing should send r1 a default route
  node: r1
  prefix: 0.0.0.0/0
  protocol: bgp
  present: false
```

## The run

On Linux or WSL2 with Docker and containerlab:

```bash
pipx install netdryrun
git clone https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun && cd netdryrun
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
```

This output is from the re-recorded [FRR CI guide](../guides/frr-ci.md#3-run-it-locally):

```text
Netdryrun 0.3.1: 6 checks from examples/frr-bgp-broken/netdryrun.yml
Deploying lab ndr-frr-broken (3 nodes); this usually takes 30-90 s, longer the first time images are pulled...
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.12.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: BGP session to 10.0.13.2 is established -- state is established (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: route 192.168.3.0/24 via bgp is present -- active via bgp (13.5s)
  [PASS] r1: ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 expects success -- 3/3 replies (need 2) (13.5s)
Convergence checks done; settling 10s before post-convergence checks...
  [PASS] r1: prefixes from 10.0.12.2 >= 1 and <= 10 -- 3 ipv4-unicast prefixes accepted (held 10s, 5 samples) (10.1s)
  [FAIL] r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent -- unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected) (0.2s)
Destroying lab...
FAILED: 5 passed, 1 failed (6 checks)
```

Exit code `1`. In the 0.3.1 release check, the same example took 39 seconds from deploy to destroy, with the images already pulled ([`live.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/releases/0.3.1/gate/live.json)).

## The diff against a ping-only check

Five of the six checks passed. Split them by what a common pre-change test looks at:

| Check | Result | Ping-only test | Sessions-up test | This file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ping 192.168.3.1 from 192.168.1.1 | pass | ✓ | | ✓ |
| BGP session to r2 established | pass | | ✓ | ✓ |
| BGP session to r3 established | pass | | ✓ | ✓ |
| route to r3's LAN present | pass | | | ✓ |
| 1 to 10 prefixes from r2 | pass (3 accepted) | | | ✓ |
| no default route via BGP | **fail** | | | ✓ |
| **Verdict** | | **pass** | **pass** | **fail** |

A test made only of the ping, or only of the sessions, would have run on this same lab and passed this change. The prefix ceiling passed too: the leak added one prefix (2 became 3), well inside a range that leaves room for growth. Only the check that names the forbidden route failed.

Why the ping still works: the LANs have more specific routes, so a default changes nothing for traffic between them. And r1 doesn't even select the leaked default: containerlab gives each node a default route through its management network, which FRR sees as a kernel route with distance 0, and that beats BGP's 20. So forwarding on r1 is exactly what it was before the change.

The same pattern shows up in the [verdict corpus](../corpus.md), a benchmark of BGP changes the maintainers wrote on one FRR topology, with expected verdicts committed before any run. In [case 17](../corpus/17-default-leaked-to-peer.md), `default-originate` toward a peer, the ping-only and all-sessions-up strategies approved the change and Netdryrun's intent checks rejected it.

## The evidence

The run with `--json report.json` writes every command and its raw output next to each check. The verdict as the [MCP server](../ai-agents.md#result-and-verdict) returns it for this example, shortened to the failed check:

```json
{
  "status": "failed",
  "passed": 5,
  "failed": 1,
  "error": null,
  "inconclusive_reason": null,
  "lab": "ndr-frr-broken",
  "checks": [
    {"name": "r1: route 0.0.0.0/0 via bgp is absent", "passed": false,
     "detail": "unexpectedly present via bgp (not selected)"}
  ],
  "evidence_file": "/path/to/lab/netdryrun-report.json",
  "verdict": "DO NOT APPLY THIS CHANGE"
}
```

The raw output behind a "(not selected)" verdict looks like this. This excerpt is from a different lab with the same leak: a peer router, `peer1`, received an upstream's default route (a validation run on Netdryrun 0.3.0, committed as the test fixture [`report-real-failed-leak.json`](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/tests/fixtures/report-real-failed-leak.json). The report stores `output` as the command's text; here it is parsed and shortened to the fields that matter):

```json
{
  "node": "peer1",
  "cmd": "vtysh -c show ip route 0.0.0.0/0 json",
  "rc": 0,
  "output": {
    "0.0.0.0/0": [
      {"protocol": "bgp", "distance": 20,
       "nexthops": [{"ip": "10.0.3.1", "interfaceName": "eth1", "active": true}]},
      {"protocol": "kernel", "selected": true, "installed": true, "distance": 0,
       "nexthops": [{"ip": "172.20.20.1", "interfaceName": "eth0", "active": true}]}
    ]
  }
}
```

Two entries for `0.0.0.0/0`. The BGP one, from the neighbor at `10.0.3.1`, has no `selected` or `installed`. The kernel one, containerlab's management default through `eth0`, is selected and installed. A check that asks "what does the router forward with?" sees only the kernel route. Netdryrun's `present: false` counts any BGP path the router received, selected or not, and fails.

To look at it yourself, rerun with `--keep-on-failure` and query the router, then destroy the lab with the command Netdryrun prints:

```bash
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken --keep-on-failure
docker exec clab-ndr-frr-broken-r1 vtysh -c "show ip route 0.0.0.0/0"
docker exec clab-ndr-frr-broken-r1 vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast 0.0.0.0/0"
```

## Why it matters if nothing changed

In this lab the leak is harmless today. It stops being harmless when the route it loses to goes away: a link fails, someone cleans up a static default, a device without a management default runs the same config. Then the received default becomes the best route, and all traffic with no more specific route goes to the neighbor that leaked it. The [hidden-leak lab](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/tree/main/examples/srl-hidden-leak) shows the same leak on Nokia SR Linux and FRR, how to see it by hand in each CLI, and what happens when the static default goes away.

A static analyzer such as Batfish also catches this particular leak, from the configs alone. The [Batfish page](../batfish.md) shows a leak it misses and the lab catches.

## Try it without installing anything

[Open Netdryrun in GitHub Codespaces](https://codespaces.new/netdryrun/Netdryrun?quickstart=1) and click **Create codespace**. It comes with Docker, containerlab and Netdryrun, and pulls the FRR image. When the terminal shows `Ready`, run:

```bash
netdryrun run examples/frr-bgp-broken
```

It uses your GitHub account's free Codespaces hours (2-core machine). Stop or delete the codespace when you're done.

To add the same check to a lab you already have, see [Add Netdryrun to the lab you already have](../guides/your-lab.md). More guards like this one are on [Guard recipes](../recipes.md).

## What a lab can't prove

This run shows one thing: in this lab, with these configs, r1 received a default route over BGP that it shouldn't have, and the check that names it caught it. It does not show:

- **That your network is free of leaks.** The check knows about `0.0.0.0/0` and nothing else. A leak of any other prefix needs its own check, or a prefix ceiling tight enough to notice it. A pass covers the checks in the file and nothing more.
- **That your vendor behaves like FRR.** The lab ran FRR containers. Route selection, defaults and timers on the routers you run in production can differ.
- **Behavior at production scale.** Three routers and a handful of prefixes say nothing about full tables, many peers, hardware or ASIC limits, or convergence time at scale.
- **What production traffic would do.** Ping tests a path between two addresses you choose; it's evidence for that path only.

More in [what a lab cannot prove](../trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove). A lab run is evidence for one change in one lab, and a reviewer can read every command and output behind it.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/trust/

# Trust and security

## License

Netdryrun™ is open source under the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/LICENSE). The source is at [github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun).

## How releases are published

- Releases are built and published by a GitHub Actions workflow when a version tag (`v*`) is pushed. The workflow checks that the tag matches the package version before building.
- Packages are uploaded to [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/netdryrun/) with **Trusted Publishing** (OpenID Connect). No PyPI token or password is stored in the repository or its secrets; PyPI accepts the upload because it comes from that workflow in that repository.
- The same workflow creates a GitHub release with the built files attached.
- The GitHub Action (`netdryrun/Netdryrun@v0.4.0`) installs Netdryrun from the action's own source at the tag you reference. Pin a tag or a commit SHA.

## Reporting a security issue

Email **[security@netdryrun.com](mailto:security@netdryrun.com)**. Please do not open a public issue for a vulnerability. Include the version, what you found, and how to reproduce it.

Advisories: every false pass we have found, in our own audits and games before any outside user reported it:

| Version | What could pass wrongly | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3.0 | A check could pass without testing what the file said | Fixed in 0.3.1; 0.3.0 is yanked on PyPI. [Advisory](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/advisories/0.3.0-false-pass/README.md) |
| 0.3.2 and earlier | An FRR config line the router rejected at boot was skipped silently | Fixed in 0.3.3. [Advisory](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/advisories/0.3.2-rejected-config/README.md) |
| 0.3.3 and earlier | A failed topology `exec:` command left the lab without that config | Fixed in 0.4.0. [Advisory](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/advisories/0.3.3-exec-not-checked/README.md) |
| 0.3.3 and earlier | On Arista EOS, `med: 0` passed on a path received with no MED (cEOS prints MED 0 for both) | Fixed in 0.4.0: a `med: 0` check on EOS is refused. [Changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) |

## What a lab cannot prove

A Netdryrun pass means the change behaved correctly in a lab. The lab runs real routing software, so a pass is strong evidence for protocol logic and policy intent: sessions come up, the intended prefixes are accepted, routes land in the routing table, traffic gets through, and unwanted routes stay out. It does not prove:

- **Vendor-specific behavior.** Open-source and container routers (FRR, SR Linux, SONiC VS) are not your vendor's routers, and even Arista cEOS is not the same as EOS on hardware. Defaults, policy evaluation and bugs differ between implementations and versions. For Arista you can bring your own licensed cEOS image.
- **Scale.** A lab has a handful of nodes and small tables, not full Internet tables or hundreds of peers.
- **Hardware and ASIC behavior.** Containers have no forwarding hardware, so TCAM limits, hardware programming and line-rate effects are not tested.
- **Config the NOS skipped.** A config line rejected at boot makes the run an error on FRR and Arista cEOS (each lists what it skipped), SR Linux fails containerlab's deploy on one, and SONiC is configured by checked `setup:` commands (a config bound into it is an error). On Juniper (beta) the load is not verified yet, and the report says so: add a positive check for what each changed line creates.
- **Timing at scale.** Convergence time in a small lab says little about convergence time in a large production network.


Version 0.4.0 also covers only BGP (IPv4/IPv6 unicast), routes, BGP best-path attributes and ping, plus link-down, node-isolation and route-injection (FRR only) failure scenarios. OSPF/IS-IS adjacencies and path checks are not covered yet.


## Running untrusted labs

containerlab runs privileged containers, so a topology and its configs are code that runs with root on the host. Only run labs you trust. In CI, see the [GitHub Action security notes](github-action.md#security-notes). For AI agents, see the [MCP safety model](ai-agents.md#safety-model).

What follows from that, by design:

- **`netdryrun.yml` is code too.** `nodes.<node>.setup` commands are shell commands run inside the node, and a `netdryrun.yml` can point at a topology in any folder. Review a `netdryrun.yml` the way you review a topology.
- **Everything else in `netdryrun.yml` is data.** From 0.3.1, VRF and interface names are restricted to letters, digits and a few punctuation marks before they reach a device CLI, and addresses and prefixes must parse as IP. A check can't run a device command it doesn't name.
- **`as_path_regex` runs with no time limit.** A pathological pattern can stall a run until your CI job's timeout; it can't do anything else. Set `timeout-minutes` on the job.
- **Text from a lab is treated as untrusted** wherever it ends up (0.3.1 and later): escaped in PR comments and step summaries, kept to one comment line in a recorded baseline, and flattened and capped in MCP results.

## Privacy

**The tool has no telemetry.** The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server do not phone home or send usage data anywhere. Reports are written only to the files you ask for (and to the GitHub Actions step summary when running in Actions). containerlab and Docker may pull images from registries named in your topology, as they normally would.

The GitHub Action has a `cloud` input reserved for a future hosted service, Netdryrun Cloud. **Netdryrun Cloud is not available yet**: its address doesn't exist, so setting `cloud: true` today uploads nothing and only adds an "evidence upload failed" warning. If it launches, uploading will stay opt-in, and its privacy terms will be published first. Leave `cloud` off.

**No AI inside the tool.** The CLI, the GitHub Action and the MCP server contain no AI model and call no AI service; verdicts come from checks run against your lab. When an AI agent uses the MCP server, the agent sends whatever it chooses to the model provider *you* picked; Netdryrun is not part of that path.

**Configs you send us.** Design partners keep their configs on their side by default; the lab runs on their machine or CI runner. If a [design partner](design-partners.md) opts in to sending us sanitized configs, they are processed with Anthropic's Claude to build their lab, under terms that don't allow training on them, and with no other AI service. They are deleted within 30 days after delivery unless the partner asks us to keep them. There are no paid products yet. See the [privacy notice](privacy.md#configs-you-send-us).

**This website** is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. It sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself, so your browser contacts no third party. GitHub, as the host, receives your IP address and request details to serve the pages.

## Trademarks

"Netdryrun" and the Netdryrun logos are trademarks of the Netdryrun project. The Apache-2.0 license covers the code, not the name: forks are welcome under a different name. See the [trademark policy](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/TRADEMARKS.md).


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/support/

# Support and versioning policy

## Support

Netdryrun is free open-source software under Apache-2.0, provided as is. Support for free use is best effort through [GitHub issues](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/issues). Security reports get priority (see [Contact](contact.md)). There is no uptime or response-time guarantee for free use.

Only the latest release gets fixes. Upgrading is the fix for bugs in older releases.

## Version numbers

Netdryrun uses [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). Before 1.0, a minor release (0.2 to 0.3) may contain breaking changes; patch releases (0.2.0 to 0.2.1) never do. Every change is in the [changelog](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## What counts as a breaking change

These are the interfaces other tools and agents rely on:

| Interface | Stable contract |
|---|---|
| CLI | command names, flags, and exit codes (`0` passed, `1` failed, `2` error, `3` inconclusive) |
| `netdryrun.yml` | check types and keys; a file that validated keeps validating |
| JSON report | the `schema` field (`netdryrun.report/v1`); fields are only added within a schema version, never removed or renamed |
| GitHub Action | input and output names and their meaning; pin a tag or a commit SHA |
| MCP server | tool names, their arguments, and the `status` and `verdict` fields |

Removing or renaming any of these, or changing their meaning, is a breaking change. Adding is not: a new check type, a new report field, or a new `status` value (`inconclusive` was added after 0.2.0). Treat any status you don't know as not passed.

## Deprecation

Before something is removed, it keeps working for at least one minor release with a warning that names the replacement, and the changelog says so. After 1.0, removals wait for the next major version.


---
Source: https://netdryrun.com/design-partners/

# Design partners

Netdryrun was first released in October 2026, and we're looking for the first outside engineers to try it on a real change. We want it shaped by real changes, not guesses. If you have a routing change coming up, we'll help you test it in a lab, for free, in exchange for honest feedback.

## What you get

- A runnable containerlab lab of the relevant part of your network, built with you on your own machine or CI runner, so your configs stay on your side.
- A `netdryrun.yml` with checks for what your change must do and what must never happen (leaks, lost reachability).
- The verdict with evidence, before your change goes anywhere real. You keep everything.
- Help wiring it into your CI, if you want it there.

Run Cisco IOS XE or IOS XR under your own Cisco licence? Help us verify the upcoming Cisco drivers on your image, and get the verdicts first.

## What we ask

- One real upcoming change. You run the lab on your side and share only what you choose: the results, a check file, the error you got stuck on. If you'd rather we build the lab for you, send sanitized configs instead (public addresses and AS numbers replaced with documentation ranges, secrets removed); we'll help you check.
- Honest feedback: what was useful, what got in the way, how you test changes today.
- Optional: permission to publish an anonymized write-up. Nothing is published without your written OK.

## Fair warning

- A lab is not production. A pass covers the checks in the lab, on the network OSes we support ([FRR, Nokia SR Linux, SONiC, Arista EOS](reference/config.md#drivers)). See [what a lab cannot prove](trust.md#what-a-lab-cannot-prove).
- We never touch your production network and never need access to it.
- We take a few partners at a time, so each change gets proper attention.

## How your configs are handled

**By default, your configs stay on your side.** The lab runs on your machine or your CI runner with your images, and nothing in Netdryrun sends your configs anywhere.

Sending us configs is opt-in. If you want us to build the lab for you, send sanitized configs only. They're used for your lab and nothing else and kept private. We build labs with the help of Anthropic's Claude, so configs you send are processed by it, under terms that don't allow training on them; no other AI service sees them. They're deleted within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. An NDA is available on request. See the [privacy notice](privacy.md#configs-you-send-us).

A Test my change issue is public: post only what you're happy to publish.

## After the free test

If it was useful and you want it on more of your network, we offer a fixed-scope paid pilot: two weeks on your runner with your images, a written check suite for your changes, and an evidence report. Your configs stay on your side. We take one pilot at a time. Ask at [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com).

## Apply

**Quickest:** open a [Test my change](https://github.com/netdryrun/Netdryrun/issues/new?template=test-my-change.yml) issue with a sanitized change. We reply there with the verdict and evidence, usually within two working days, and you tell us whether it was right.

Or run `netdryrun feedback` and tick "Design partner", or email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com) with one line about the change you want to test.

Source: https://netdryrun.com/contact/

# Privacy notice

*Last updated: 27 October 2026*

## Who is responsible

Netdryrun is operated by Victor Khen, Taiwan ("we"). Contact for anything about your data: [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com).

## The short version

- **The Netdryrun tool** (CLI, GitHub Action, MCP server) has no telemetry. It sends us nothing. The GitHub Action has a `cloud` input reserved for Netdryrun Cloud, a hosted service that is not available yet; setting it today uploads nothing. Its own privacy terms will be published here before it launches.
- **This website** sets no cookies, has no analytics and no forms, and serves its fonts itself.
- **We see your data only if you email us, interact with the project on GitHub, or send us configs as a design partner.**

## This website

netdryrun.com is static documentation hosted on GitHub Pages. To deliver the pages, GitHub processes your IP address and request details (page, time, browser) under the [GitHub privacy statement](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement). We do not receive these logs. If you switch between light and dark mode, your browser remembers the choice in its local storage; that stays on your device. Search runs entirely in your browser.

## Email

When you write to an @netdryrun.com address, Cloudflare Email Routing forwards the message to our mailbox. Mail we send from an @netdryrun.com address goes out through Resend, an email delivery service, which handles the recipient address and message to deliver it. We use your address and message only to answer you and keep the conversation for as long as it's useful, then delete it. Security reports may be kept as records of how the issue was handled. Lawful basis: our legitimate interest in answering you.

## Configs you send us

If you are a [design partner](design-partners.md), your configs stay on your side by default: the lab runs on your machine or CI runner, and we see only what you choose to share. If you opt in to sending us sanitized configs so we can build a lab of part of your network, we use them only for your lab. We build labs with the help of Anthropic's Claude, so Anthropic processes the configs on our behalf, under commercial terms that don't allow training on them; no other AI service receives them. We delete them within 30 days after delivery unless you ask us to keep them. Lawful basis: your request (the work you asked us to do).

## GitHub and PyPI

Issues, pull requests and discussions on [github.com/netdryrun](https://github.com/netdryrun) are public and governed by GitHub's terms and privacy statement. Downloads from PyPI are handled by the Python Software Foundation under the [PyPI privacy notice](https://policies.python.org/pypi.org/Privacy-Notice/). We don't combine this information with anything else.

## Transfers

GitHub, Cloudflare, Resend and Anthropic are based in the United States. Transfers of personal data from the EU or UK rely on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (and its UK extension) where the company is certified, and on the European Commission's standard contractual clauses otherwise.

## Your rights

You can ask for access to, correction of, or deletion of your personal data, a copy of it, restriction of processing, or object to processing based on legitimate interest. Email [hello@netdryrun.com](mailto:hello@netdryrun.com); we answer within 30 days. You can also complain to your data protection authority.

## Changes

We update this notice when what we do with data changes, for example before Netdryrun Cloud or paid products launch, and change the date at the top.
